findings.problem: The TLDR says the 747 "crossed New York to London eastbound in 4 h 56 min, at a ground speed of 1,327 km/h against an airspeed of 933." 1,327 km/h was the PEAK, not the crossing speed: the body itself says "an average ground speed of 1,126 km/h and a peak of 1,327 km/h", and Guinness says the aircraft reached "a speed of 1,327 km/h (825 mph) relative to the ground below". The TLDR's own numbers do not close — 5,554 km at 1,327 km/h is 4 h 11 min, not 4 h 56. This is the recurring failure the sweep report names twice (TLDR written from memory of the argument, stronger than the body), and it is in the field a reader sees before anything else and may never expand past.
findings.fix: Replace "at a ground speed of 1,327 km/h against an airspeed of 933" with "averaging 1,126 km/h over the ground and peaking at 1,327, against an airspeed of about 933".

findings.field: clusters.py A08 (renders into this entry's header and refutation summary)
findings.problem: clusters.py A08 still carries originator="Samuel Rowbotham", originator_work="Earth Not a Globe", year="1865", and note="Descends from Rowbotham's vertical-projectile argument. The atmosphere co-moves; INS platforms explicitly correct for a ~15 deg/hr Earth rate." render.py prints the originator in the meta line ("first published by …") directly above this treatment, and prints the cluster note as the refutation panel's summary line (build.py:161 maps note to basis; render.py renders basis under the "3 · Refutation" chip). So as shipped the page says "first published by Samuel Rowbotham" immediately above a gloss arguing the aeroplane argument cannot be Rowbotham's (he died 23 Dec 1884; powered flight 17 Dec 1903 — both verified), and summarises the refutation with "the atmosphere co-moves", the exact answer the entry's own steelman labels SURFACE and says "loses, and it deserves to". The file reports this upward in docstring note 10 and correctly does not edit another file, so this is a process defect, not a writing one — but it is unapplied, and it is the fifth recurrence of the E01/E03 pattern.
findings.fix: Owner outside this file: anchor the edit on the cluster key "A08" (never on the byte-identical originator= line), set the originator state deliberately — Henriet is the earliest text LOCATED, not a demonstrated first author, so untraced is the honest value unless a PER-HENRIET/WRK record is created and priority verified — and rewrite the note to lead with the alignment procedure rather than co-rotation. Then update tests/test_provenance.py: Rowbotham 65 → 61 items, plus the named-originator count and the Rowbotham+Sungenis 43% assertion.

findings.problem: Both fields say Henriet writes "kilometers" three times and Dubay prints "miles" three times. Inside the block Dubay reproduces it is FOUR times each: "1,000 kilometers an hour", "only 500 kilometers", "a distance of 1,500 kilometers", "such a flying speed of 1,000 kilometers an hour" — all four printed as miles. Henriet's fuller passage has a fifth ("an airfield which is slipping away at the rate of 1,000 kilometers an hour"), which the gloss itself quotes. The entry bills this substitution as its sharpest single finding; a defender with both texts open will find the count wrong on the first check.
findings.fix: "four times" in both fields, or "at every occurrence in the block he reproduces — four of them".

findings.field: compression.note ("verified in two independent copies of each book")
findings.problem: For Henriet this is true (archive.org item HeavenAndEarthGabrielleHenriet and the theflatearthsociety.org PDF — I confirmed "kilometers" in the second). For Dubay it is not: the file's own docstring note 4 says the two checks were "the djvu OCR and … the PDF text layer" of one Internet Archive item (200-proofs-the-earth-is-not-a-spinning-ball). Those are two derivations of a single scan, not two copies. On a page whose product is provenance rigour, overstating a verification claim is the most expensive kind of small error.
findings.fix: "verified in two independent copies of Henriet and in two text layers of the Internet Archive scan of Dubay".

findings.problem: The field is written with HTML entities (“, ”, —) but render.py escapes it: line 242 emits e(d["straw_man"]["detail"]) where e() is html.escape. The published paragraph will therefore read: gravity “magically and inexplicably drags the entire lower-atmosphere … infinite vacuum space.” — literal entity text throughout, in the one panel where we accuse the source of caricature. Every other treatment file writes literal typographic characters here; A08 and A19 are the only two that do not.
findings.fix: Replace “/”/— in straw_man.detail with the literal characters “ ” —, as _b8_R03.py and deep.py's A03 do.

findings.problem: The gloss says "East/west symmetry as a numbered proof is in One Hundred Proofs (1885) twice over" and then cites proof 44 and proof 54. Proof 54 (verified verbatim in Gutenberg #55387) is the balloon-not-left-behind argument and contains no east/west comparison at all — it is a vehicle-decoupling claim, the same family as the air-gun. The genuine second instance is proof 42 ("Projectiles--firing east or west": "there would unquestionably be a difference in the result of firing off a projectile in that direction and in a direction the opposite of that one. But as, in fact, there is not the slightest difference…"), which the docstring identifies but the published gloss drops. A defender who opens the cited Gutenberg text finds our claimed ancestry citing a proof that never mentions east or west.
findings.fix: "…is in One Hundred Proofs (1885) twice over — proof 42 and, restated with a figure, proof 44", then keep proof 54 introduced as what it is: the balloon form of the same decoupling argument.

findings.problem: unsourced_addition is justified on the ground that "the symmetry claim is attributed to a literature in which this pass could not locate it". But Dubay proof 24 — one item before the quoted run, in the same book — asserts directional symmetry as observed fact: "regardless of which direction cannons are fired, the distance covered is always the same." Carpenter proof 44, quoted in our own gloss, asserts it too ("there is not the slightest difference, whichever way the thing may be done"). By the entry's own genealogical logic (docstring: "the vehicle is a cannon and a balloon because those were the vehicles") the symmetry claim IS in that literature, with a different vehicle. The entry quotes proofs 23, 25, 26 and 27 and never mentions 24, the nearest counter-example to its own classification.
findings.fix: Address proof 24 in the note and say why cannon symmetry is not flight-time symmetry, or reclassify as scope_widened (which the note already offers as the alternative) and keep unsourced_addition only for item 13's "navigation not compensating".

findings.field: refutation section 1 ("westbound traffic detoured north of Greenland")
findings.problem: "On the same day westbound traffic detoured north of Greenland to escape the headwind and lost more than an hour." No source in the sources list carries this: the Guinness page covers only the eastbound record (confirmed on fetch), and the CNN piece has nothing about 9 February westbound routings (confirmed on fetch). The supporting source is the Flightradar24 record-flight post, cited in docstring note 5 but absent from sources. That post also says less than we do: "flights are routing to the north of the jet stream over Greenland" and "Some flights are adding more than 60 minutes, while others that manage to avoid the jet stream entirely are in some cases arriving early." We flatten "some flights" into "westbound traffic" and drop the early arrivals — a small compression of a hedged source, in an entry about compression of hedged sources.
findings.fix: Add the Flightradar24 post to sources and rewrite as: "the same day, westbound flights were routing north of the jet stream over Greenland, some adding more than an hour."

findings.problem: https://digilander.libero.it/andreatheone/irs.htm returns HTTP 410 Gone (checked twice this run, default and browser user-agent; the Libero portal page is served instead), and the Wayback availability API returned no snapshot for it. This is the load-bearing citation for the entry's headline TLDR claim and for five quoted sentences in section 3. The text itself is fine — I verified every quoted sentence, including "These comparisons must be favorable to complete the alignment period", against a live mirror carrying the identical document.
findings.fix: Cite http://b767ops.blogspot.com/2014/06/about-irss-and-how-they-work.html (live, same text, same five sentences) alongside or instead of the digilander URL, keeping the "unofficial mirror" disclosure and the Inside GNSS corroboration.

findings.problem: Section 5 states flatly that Coriolis, Eötvös, sensed Earth rate and the clock split are "four quantities that are zero on a stationary Earth", and section 4 says the Hafele–Keating split "exists only because the ground the aircraft take off from is itself moving". The entry's own advocate rates the rotating-cosmos reply 4/5 and its preemptive (c) commits to conceding it "in the body with a cross-link to ARG-R01 and ARG-R03" — narrowly, because neither list claim survives the concession. That concession is not in the body: the refutation cross-links R03 only for the weaker Galilean cancelling point and never mentions R01. And build.py strips advocate from the published deep (it is written to review/advocate.json), so a reader sees the unqualified claim and never the concession. The physics is right; the strongest attack on the entry is answered only where readers cannot see it.
findings.fix: Add two sentences to section 5: concede that the gyro, Coriolis and clock results measure rotation relative to the local inertial frame and are observationally equivalent under a rotating-cosmos model (link ARG-R01 and ARG-R03), then narrow — "flight times symmetric" is false in the timetables and "navigation not compensating" is false in the alignment procedure whatever defines that frame.

findings.problem: "This is the same instrument, and the same 15°/hr, that ARG-A07 records a flat-earth researcher measuring on camera and declining to accept." Two problems. (a) "The same instrument" follows immediately after naming the Honeywell GG1320AN; _b8_A07.py identifies no model for Knodel's gyro and deliberately withholds even the widely-quoted price line, so we have no basis for identity of instrument, only of type. (b) "Declining to accept" is the framing A07 explicitly abandons: A07 credits the systematics hunt as "correct practice", locates its finding in a missing acceptance criterion, and lists "you have written it up as refusing to accept data" as the defender's charge against us. Knodel is living, and A07 is scrupulous about it; A08 reimports the framing in one clause.
findings.fix: "This is the same quantity, and the same instrument class — a navigation-grade ring laser gyro — that ARG-A07 records reading 15°/hr on camera, where the finding is the missing acceptance criterion rather than the reading."

findings.problem: The paragraph that answers our own KERNEL ends: "The entrainment hypothesis got its altitude and its independent replication, and neither produced Miller's signal." The Joos half is sourced. The altitude half is not, and the source we cite for the move supplies no result: Swenson p. 225 records the summer-1930 installation in the base of the 100-inch and then goes straight to Joos, and his note 29 says the opposite of a clean outcome — correspondence of January 1930 "indicates that Michelson had lost interest by then and that the latest observational data was not suitable for publication." I could find no published result from the Mount Wilson installation. So our answer to the defender's strongest point asserts an experimental outcome we cannot cite, in a field whose whole job is to be unimpeachable. Miller's heir says in one line: the mountain data was never published, so you cannot quote it against me.
findings.fix: Rewrite the concession honestly: "Acted on: in the summer of 1930 Pease and Pearson had the instrument carried up the mountain and installed in the base of the 100-inch telescope — the elevation Miller asked for. No result from that installation is reported in Swenson's account, whose note records that by January 1930 Michelson had lost interest and that the latest data was 'not suitable for publication'. What answered the objection was Joos, who in the same season ran a 21-metre interferometer at Jena, in Miller's own direct response, and reported an effect 'less than 1/1000 of a fringe width ... less than 1.5 km/sec'." That is both true and stronger, because it concedes the loose end before a defender finds it.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py A11 note (renders as the Refutation summary line inside this card, render.py:180)
findings.problem: The cluster note reads "A high-precision repeat of Michelson–Morley (expected 0.9 fringe, measured 0.01), run by Michelson at Mount Wilson specifically to test Miller." build.py:161 maps note -> basis and render.py:180 prints basis as the summary line of section 3, directly above a refutation whose section 2 is headed "The higher altitude did not happen" and states the site was Pasadena. Two of that sentence's three factual claims are wrong on our own evidence: the site was the observatory's Pasadena laboratory (Miller 1933 RMP 5:240; Swenson pp. 220-221; the comparison table's own location field, "Pasadena (Mt. Wilson optical shop)"), and Pease and Pearson did the observing under Michelson's supervision. A reader who never expands the card sees only the wrong version. The docstring (note 11b) reports this and does not fix it — the E01/E03 "recorded, not applied" pattern, on the one fact this entry is distinctive for.
findings.fix: Operator action, anchored on the cluster key "A11" and never on the originator= line: note="A high-precision repeat of Michelson–Morley (expected 0.9 fringe, measured 0.01), run by Pease and Pearson under Michelson at the Mount Wilson Observatory's Pasadena laboratory, specifically to test Miller. Same non-discriminating status as A01." While there, real_source should carry both printings — the sentence the whole downstream tradition quotes is the Nature note of 19 Jan 1929, and the two printings give different ratios.

findings.problem: The opening sentence asserts "the chain that carried it to this list turned that into a detection of 20 km/s". The body twice refuses that claim: the gloss says "the specimen carries no citation for item 10 ... so which text its compiler read is not something this page can show", the compression note repeats it, and verdict_challenge names it as the challenge's weak point ("we cannot show the compiler read this book rather than a textbook table that calls the result null"). The TLDR also sits oddly against its own third sentence — if the chain turned the null into a detection, the list would not be "the more orthodox party". This is the recurring failure: the summary claims a provenance the argument below it declines to claim, and the TLDR is escaped and rendered first, above everything that qualifies it.
findings.fix: Make the TLDR describe the tradition rather than a delivery path: "The 1929 experiment reported an upper limit ... and the geocentric literature this item is traced to turned that into a detection of 20 km/s by dividing 300 by 15, when a Michelson-Morley fringe shift goes as the square of the speed." One word ('literature' for 'chain that carried it to this list') removes a claim the page cannot support and costs the sentence nothing.

findings.problem: "the modern descendants are rotating optical cavities, which bound the anisotropy of the speed of light at Δc/c ≈ 10⁻¹⁷ (Herrmann et al. 2009) and 10⁻¹⁸ (Nagel et al. 2015) — fifteen orders of magnitude past 1929". The two bounds and both arXiv IDs are correct (1002.1284 = PRD 80:105011 2009; 1412.6954 = Nat. Commun. 6:8174 2015). The 'fifteen' is not. It appears to come from comparing the 1929 fringe-shift bound (0.01) with a fractional anisotropy (10⁻¹⁷) — different quantities. In the same units, 1929's v ≤ 3.1 km/s corresponds to Δc/c ~ (v/c)² ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰, so the gain to 10⁻¹⁸ is about eight orders, not fifteen. A hostile reader checks exactly this kind of flourish, and eight orders is already overwhelming.
findings.fix: "...at Δc/c ≈ 10⁻¹⁷ and 10⁻¹⁸ — eight orders of magnitude past the 1929 bound, whose v ≤ 3 km/s corresponds to Δc/c of about 10⁻¹⁰ — still null, still exactly what relativity predicts for an Earth in motion."

findings.field: refutation, section 1, third paragraph (and passage.gloss, fourth paragraph)
findings.problem: We quote Swenson to establish the two-printing discrepancy and stop one clause short. His sentence (p. 222) reads in full: "Later, in March, the Journal of the Optical Society of America reported that nothing was observed within one-fiftieth of the expected shift, based on Sternberg's estimate of the solar system's resultant velocity of about three thousand kilometers per second." Our text cuts at 'expected shift'. The omitted clause is material to the arithmetic on the same page: the gloss prints Munera's 42.4 km/s for the JOSA figure, which is 300/√50 and presupposes the 300 km/s basis Swenson explicitly does not give it. So in the passage whose point is that the book prints three unreconciled velocities without noticing, we print a derived velocity our own cited historian contradicts, and we truncate him at the clause that would show it. Neither of the two 1929 printings was reached (the entry says so), so this is the only evidence we have on the question.
findings.fix: Restore the clause and turn it into a point: "...reported that nothing was observed within one-fiftieth of the expected shift — 'based on Sternberg's estimate of the solar system's resultant velocity of about three thousand kilometers per second', which is not the 300 km/s the Nature figure references, so Munera's 42.4 km/s for the JOSA printing rests on a basis Swenson's account does not support. Neither printing was reached for this entry; the ratios are as reported by Swenson and Munera." Also drop 'the record is clear' from the paragraph's opening — the record is documented, not clear.

findings.problem: "The book treats this experiment as a Michelson-Morley repetition about translation through the ether, and puts rotation elsewhere — in Michelson-Gale and Sagnac ... Nothing in its pages on Michelson-Pease-Pearson locates a rotation claim." Our own refutation section 5 quotes footnote 752 — "It is precisely the rotation of the ether every 24 hours that accounts for the small positive results of all the interferometer experiments at the surface of the Earth" — and that footnote sits at the foot of printed p. 387, i.e. inside the pages the note says contain no rotation claim, attached to the Michelson-Pease-Pearson discussion and expressly covering 'all the interferometer experiments'. Two published fields of the same entry contradict each other, and it happens in the compression block, which is the project's flagship finding field. It is also an absence claim scoped only to 'its pages on Michelson-Pease-Pearson' — no edition, no page range, no route — which is weaker than the rule asks even where it is true.
findings.fix: "No claim that this experiment measured the Earth's rotation is located in the archive.org OCR's pages on Michelson-Pease-Pearson (printed pp. 385–387) or at the 'null' mention on p. 353. Rotation does appear there, but as the book's explanation rather than as the experiment's subject: footnote 752, at the foot of p. 387, credits 'the rotation of the ether every 24 hours' with the small positive results of all the interferometer experiments — a mechanism answered on its own numbers in the refutation."

findings.field: refutation section 6, and the Wettzell entry in sources
findings.problem: "the ring laser at Wettzell ... tracks the Earth's rotation rate below one part in 10⁹ and resolves length-of-day variation and polar motion in agreement with very-long-baseline interferometry", cited to Eur. Phys. J. C 82 (2022), doi 10.1140/epjc/s10052-022-10798-9. That paper ('Overcoming 1 part in 10⁹ of earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data') supports the first half — its Allan deviation drops below 1 part in 10⁹ after about 10⁴ s of integration, on two three-day data sets. It does not support the second: it contains no mention of VLBI or of length-of-day, and it treats diurnal polar motion only as a modelled correction that is subtracted, adding that those corrections 'have to be considered as preliminary'. The underlying claim is true of the ring-laser literature; it is not true of this citation, and on a project whose product is provenance, a claim attached to a paper that does not make it is the worst available error.
findings.fix: Either narrow the sentence to what the paper says ('resolves the Earth's rotation rate below one part in 10⁹ after hours of integration') or add the citation that carries the rest — Schreiber et al. on direct ring-laser measurement of polar motion, cross-checked against the IERS/VLBI series — and split the source label accordingly.

findings.field: passage.gloss / refutation / compression.source_wording / compression.note / sources[2] / docstring §3, §10
findings.problem: Six of the eight page citations to Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I are one page low against the printed page numbers in the scan the entry names (archive.org item GallileoWasWrong). Verified by mapping the item's hOCR page index to its page-number table and confirmed on the page images themselves: Bennett's ch. 12 'Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentric Cosmology' opens on printed p. 710, not 709 (page image of leaf 722 shows the chapter title above the footer '710'), and the 'Centrifugal forces cause the water and air near the equator to rise ... the polar flattening and equatorial bulge. This also explains why the acceleration of gravity is less at the equator' sentence is on that page; the 'Claims and Responses / Response: All the various effects noted above depend on the assumption...' text is on p. 711, not 710. Likewise Russell's 'the flattening of the Earth at the poles, and the fact that bodies are heavier there than at the equator' is on p. 49, not 48 (page image of leaf 61 shows footer '49'); Mach quoted in full with 'our law of inertia is wrongly expressed. I prefer the second way' is at ch. 7, p. 460, not 459; the clipped Mach quote ('...and so on...') is on p. 204, not 203 — the same page as the 'not that a rotation of the Earth is the force' sentence the entry cites correctly as p. 204; the WGS84 1/298.257223563 is in Appendix 7 at p. 1028, not 1027; and the satellite-photograph parenthesis in ch. 11 (Hildegardian Geocentrism, confirmed) is at p. 699, not 698. Only ch. 4 p. 204 and ch. 5 p. 239 n. 492 are right (the Einstein footnote is exactly n. 492 on p. 239, and it does cite Annalen der Physik 35, 903). The docstring asserts these 'are the printed numbers in the Vol. I OCR (item GallileoWasWrong)'; they are not. On a page whose product is provenance, and against an in-copyright source a hostile reader will check, a citation that lands on the wrong page is the most expensive kind of error available.
findings.fix: Renumber throughout: 709→710, 710→711, 48→49, 459→460, 203→204, 1027→1028, 698→699. Keep 204 and 239. Then change the docstring's provenance note to say the printed numbers were read from the page images of the named scan (leaves 722, 723, 61, 472, 216, 1040, 711), rather than 'not checked against a print copy', since the scan's own footers are now the evidence.

findings.problem: The TLDR says 'The thermal-expansion coefficient he quotes on the same page is about eight times too small to account for what he is explaining.' The body says the opposite, in as many words: 'The coefficient is not the problem. 1/150,000 per °F is 6.7 × 10⁻⁶/°F, against a modern figure for steel of 11.7 × 10⁻⁶/°C = 6.5 × 10⁻⁶/°F. He quoted a good number and did not multiply it out.' What is eight times too small is the effect — coefficient times his own 84.2 °F range, 0.056% against the 0.436% he has to explain. This is the sweep's recurring failure #2/#6 (TLDR written from memory of the argument), and it hands a defender a free rebuttal from our own text: the entry's centrepiece is that Rowbotham's number was good and his arithmetic absent, and the summary line contradicts it.
findings.fix: Rewrite the clause as: 'and the thermal expansion he offers as the cause — his own good coefficient times his own 84.2 °F equator-to-pole range — comes out about eight times too small to produce it.'

findings.field: passage.gloss (bolded sentence: 'Both books grant the phenomena. Neither of them asserts items 180 or 257.')
findings.problem: An unscoped absence claim about the entire contents of two books, made from the passages read — the dominant confirmed failure across both prior sweeps, and it evades the ratcheting lint only because 'neither of them asserts' is not one of the regex's shapes ('writers have learned the regex, not the rule'). Worse, the entry itself prints two counter-instances from the same volume within the next two paragraphs. At printed p. 699 the book says satellite photographs 'do not show an equatorial bulge'; at p. 711, restating Barbour and Bertotti, it says 'An object at the center of the hollow sphere will not be affected by the inertial forces. The space around the Earth will exhibit the inertial effects of the distant sphere, but not the Earth itself, if it is centrally located' — which is a source statement that no centrifugal effect acts on the Earth, i.e. very close to item 180. The affirmations at pp. 710, 204 and 49 are real and the 'reversed' drift verdict survives on them, but the flat 'neither of them asserts' does not, and a defender who reads section 5 of our own refutation can say so.
findings.fix: Replace with a scoped and honest version: 'No assertion of items 180 or 257 was located in the passages of Vol. I read for this entry — pp. 49, 204, 239, 460, 699, 710-711 and Appendix 7 — and the two sentences that come nearest, the satellite-photograph parenthesis at p. 699 and the centrally-located-Earth remark at p. 711, are both answered below. What the book does throughout is grant the phenomena and dispute their cause.' Then add a line to compression.note recording that p. 711 is the closest thing to a source for item 180 that was found, and that it contradicts the book's own p. 710.

findings.field: refutation, §2 final paragraph (cross-reference to ARG-B05); related[]
findings.problem: 'It is the same move the project records at ARG-B05, where he reproduces the Encyclopædia Britannica's correction for the curvature of the Earth and then denies the curvature it corrects for.' The subject of that sentence is Rowbotham, but clusters.py has B05 = 'Engineering makes no curvature allowance (canals, rail, pipelines, bridges)', originator William Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs, 1885 — a different author, a different book and no Britannica material. The finding described is B07 ('Refraction is invoked ad hoc to rescue curvature', Rowbotham, 1849, MISLEADING), whose treatment is built on Rowbotham reprinting the Encyclopædia Britannica 'Levelling' article with its one-seventh-of-the-curvature refraction coefficient at p. 34. The anchor is live, so a reader who clicks lands on Carpenter's canals and finds nothing of what the sentence promised.
findings.fix: Change the anchor and label to ARG-B07 and add 'B07' to related[]. Consider dropping 'B05' from related[] unless the Carpenter cluster is wanted for another reason.

findings.field: refutation, §3 first paragraph ('the French Peru and Lapland degrees (56,653 and 57,422 toises)'); docstring §6
findings.problem: The entry vouches for both figures — the docstring states they 'are the real published figures' — but only the Lapland one checks out. 57,422 toises is confirmed (and is exactly what the 1911 Britannica's Lapland arc of 55,023 toises over 57′ 29″·6 yields). The Peru figure does not: the same Britannica article gives the Peruvian arc as 176,945 toises over 3° 7′ 3″, i.e. about 56,760 toises per degree, and the figure in general circulation is 56,753. Rowbotham's 56,653 is roughly 100 toises (about 200 m) low — the same class of transposed digit as the '577 to 875' the paragraph three lines later is busy catching, and we certified it instead. The same sentence also asserts that both degrees 'did not survive later scrutiny intact'; Rowbotham's text and the sources reached here support that only for the Lapland arc.
findings.fix: Amend to: 'the Lapland degree he quotes, 57,422 toises, is the published Maupertuis figure and it did not survive the Swedish re-measurement intact; his Peru degree of 56,653 toises does not match the published Peruvian arc, which yields about 56,753-56,760 toises per degree — a second corrupt figure of the same kind as the Huygens ratio below, and a second one that inflates the disagreement his argument runs on.'

findings.field: refutation, §3 second-to-last paragraph ('overstates it by a factor of about 170')
findings.problem: The factor does not follow from any natural reading of the figures given. Rowbotham's 577:875 implies a flattening of (875−577)/875 = 0.3406, against Huygens's 1/578 = 0.001730 — a factor of about 197. Taking his own gloss ('about one-third of the whole diameter') gives 1/3 ÷ 1/578 ≈ 193. Reading 'it' as the Newton-Huygens disagreement rather than the flattening gives about 126. Nothing gives 170. The referent of 'it' is also unstated, which is half the problem: this is a published number a checker will recompute, in the one paragraph of the entry whose whole point is that an unchecked number was printed.
findings.fix: State the quantity and the arithmetic: 'his 577:875 implies a flattening of 0.34, about 197 times Huygens's actual 1/578 = 0.0017.'

findings.problem: The Noad coefficient is garbled inside a direct quotation. The HTML reads 'will alter its length ⅓<sub>5000</sub>th part', and ⅓ is U+2153 VULGAR FRACTION ONE THIRD, so the published gloss quotes Noad as saying '⅓5000th part'. The source (Gutenberg #69892, and the same sentence in the third edition) reads ¹⁄₅₀₀₀th part — one five-thousandth. The entity is two code points off (⅟ is ⅑). This is the load-bearing coefficient of the entry's centrepiece: a reader who wants to check 84.2 ÷ 150,000 cannot get 1/150,000 out of what the gloss prints, and the refutation four sections later gives the correct '1/5000 of its length for 30 °F', so the two disagree.
findings.fix: Replace with '1/5000th part' or '⅓' → '⅑<sub>5000</sub>th part', and check the rendered page rather than the entity table — the same ⅓ is used correctly as ⅓ in _b9_D19.py, which is probably where it was copied from.

findings.problem: The field that a reader meets side by side with the list's phrasing quotes, as Sungenis and Bennett's own wording, a sentence that is their statement of the geokinetic claim they are about to answer. On p. 710 the passage is introduced as 'there are three geokinetic claims for terrestrial motion' and 'All claims center on the inertial forces called centrifugal and Coriolis that explain the following effects ... based on the presumption of Earth's rotation'; the numbered item quoted is #2 in that opponent's list. The entry knows this — the gloss says 'states the geokinetic claim' and the note quotes the Response — but compression.source_wording carries the claim-statement alone with no marker, which is a small version of the move the hedge rule exists to stop, committed in our favour. The substance still holds: the Response at p. 711 concedes rather than denies, and that is what makes the drift finding stand.
findings.fix: Label it: 'Sungenis & Bennett, Vol. I ch. 12, p. 710, stating the geokinetic claim they will answer: centrifugal forces produce "the polar flattening and equatorial bulge. This also explains why the acceleration of gravity is less at the equator" — and answering it at p. 711 not by denying the effects but by writing that they "depend on the assumption that the inertial effects can only be caused by the Earth's rotation."'

findings.field: refutation, §6 ('The bulge is not stable, and the part that is unexplained does not help')
findings.problem: The section answers item 105's four-word fragment ('Stable equatorial bulge.') — no source wording for it is located anywhere in the entry — and it answers with variations whose magnitudes are never given, in an entry whose governing discipline is magnitude. The twice-daily body tide of about 30 cm is 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ of the 21.4 km bulge; the J2 reversal Cox and Chao report is of order 10⁻⁸ in relative terms, i.e. sub-millimetre on the polar-equatorial radius difference. 'It is not stable, and the ways in which it moves are among the better-measured things in geophysics' is true and well cited, but as an answer to 'stable' it is the kind of move the entry refuses to make elsewhere — and it sits three paragraphs from a passage arguing that a 113 m excess is negligible because it is half a per cent. The advocate block already anticipates the double-standard charge for the 113 m; it does not anticipate it here.
findings.fix: Add the ratios and reframe: 'the bulge is not rigid — it flexes about 30 cm twice a day, one part in 70,000 of its own size, and its dynamical measure J2 has a measured secular trend that reversed around 1998. These are small, and saying so is the point: they are exactly the size a responsive rotational figure should show, and none of them is available to an argument that needs the bulge to have a non-rotational cause.'

findings.problem: The one leg of the centrepiece not computed from the source's own numbers, and it answers a different mechanism than the one the source names. Rowbotham's second cause is resistance: 'if the pendulum vibrates in the air, which is colder and therefore denser in the north than at the equator, it must be more or less resisted in its passage through it', and his authority is Derham on the arcs of vibration in an air-pump receiver. Our reply invokes 'the buoyancy and added-mass corrections for a metal bob in air', gives no arithmetic, and asserts 'something of order a hundredth of one per cent' and 'two orders of magnitude below what is needed' with no derivation — while the steelman calls it 'several hundred times too small', a third figure. A defender gets to say we substituted a mechanism we could dismiss and then did not show the numbers, in the section whose authority comes from showing the numbers.
findings.fix: Name his mechanism and do the arithmetic in one line: buoyancy plus added mass shift the period by about ρ_air/ρ_bob ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ for a steel bob; the equator-to-pole change in sea-level air density is roughly 15-20% of that, so about 3 × 10⁻⁵ — a factor of ~150 short of 0.436%. Then note that damping, the effect Derham actually measured, changes amplitude and reaches the period only through the circular-error term, which is smaller still. Make the steelman's 'several hundred' agree with whichever number is published.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py :: A14 originator / originator_work / year / real_source / note (renders inside this entry)
findings.problem: The cluster record contradicts the treatment it renders around. It credits originator="Samuel Rowbotham", originator_work="Earth Not a Globe", year="1865" — and I confirmed the attribution fails: the Project Gutenberg text of the 1865 Simpkin Marshall edition (#69892) returns 0 hits for artiller, gunner, cannon, ballist, projectile and mortar, and the only projectile passage is the vertical air-gun, which assign.py already routes to A08. The header will therefore print "first published by Samuel Rowbotham" directly above a gloss that says "the argument is older than anyone on the People tab, and no single author is credited for it here". Worse, the cluster note — "Long-range gunnery has corrected for Coriolis drift since WWI; naval fire-control computers did it mechanically" — renders as the basis line under the Refutation summary, immediately above our own concession that the word Coriolis is not located in the 2016 manual, and the entry's docstring says neither half of that note was verified and the WWI half failed a check against Alger 1917. Reported up in docstring section 10, not applied: the E01/E03 'recorded, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED' pattern.
findings.fix: Batch owner (not this file) edits scripts/clusters.py, anchored on the cluster key "A14" and never on the byte-identical originator= line: originator/originator_work/year -> None, add pre_modern=dict(earliest_documented_use="Riccioli, Almagestum Novum (Bologna, 1651), Part II bk 9 sec. 4 ch. 21, pp. 425, 426-7 — arguments 17 and 19 of his 77", repopularised=["Eric Dubay 2015", "Edward Hendrie 2016"]) with no use of the word "first" (tests enforce both); real_source="TC 3-09.81 (2016) Tables H and I; FM 6-40 (1945) firing-table tables D and E"; note="US Army firing tables have carried a rotation-of-the-earth correction, indexed by the latitude of the battery, since at least 1945; the 2016 cannon gunnery manual publishes the deflection half in mils."

findings.problem: The note asserts that "Artillery stationary calculations" and "Artillery geocentric mils" are both additions the list made — "Neither statement is located in proof 24 of 200 Proofs" — and drift_type="unsourced_addition" is set for the cluster. But the entry itself identifies Hendrie, not Dubay, as the source of the word "artillery", and the test was run only against Dubay. Hendrie p. 112 (verified in the archive OCR) reads: "then the artillery officers and snipers would be trained to consider the spin of the earth in making their calculations for accurate firing. Yet, you will look in vain for any mention of Coriolis effect in any military artillery or sniper instruction manual." Item 114 is a faithful compression of that sentence. So we publish, under the panel heading "The list overstates its own source", a provenance finding that is wrong on one of the two items it names — the mirror image of the sin the hedge rule exists to prevent. (The mils half is sound: I confirmed "mils" occurs 0 times in the OCR of both books.) Secondary: the panel heading reads "The list overstates its own source" while the note's first bolded sentence says the central item does not overstate it.
findings.fix: Split the classification in compression.note and lead with the addition that justifies the panel. Replace the second paragraph's opening with: "Of the other two items, one is an addition and one is not. “Artillery geocentric mils” is the list’s own vocabulary: the word mils is not located anywhere in the archive.org OCR text of either book searched for this entry. “Artillery stationary calculations” is not an addition — it compresses Hendrie at p. 112, where the artillery officers who would be “trained to consider the spin of the earth in making their calculations for accurate firing” are said not to be." Keep drift_type="unsourced_addition" (it is still true of item 407) and let the note carry the split, as the enum is a convenience rather than a theory.

findings.field: refutation, section 2 bullet 2 ("four orders below"); echoed in advocate.best_defense
findings.problem: "Its magnitude is four orders below the effect the claim looks for" is not reproducible from the entry's own numbers. Using the entry's own 155 mm case: the naive model it just described (447 m/s added to and subtracted from a 684 m/s muzzle velocity, range as v^2) gives an eastward range of ~60 km against a westward ~2.6 km, so a predicted east/west difference of ~57 km; the real difference is 2 x 78 m = 156 m. That is a factor of ~370, i.e. 2.6 orders. One-sided it is ~2.9 orders. The only way to reach four is to compare the dimensionless 23:1 ratio against the 0.36% fractional shift, which is not a like-for-like comparison. On a page whose authority rests on arithmetic it computed itself, a headline order-of-magnitude claim overstated by more than a full order is the kind of thing a paid skeptic checks first.
findings.fix: Replace "Its magnitude is four orders below the effect the claim looks for" with a concrete pairing: "The naive version predicts an east/west range difference of tens of kilometres at this range; the real one is about 150 metres — smaller by a factor of several hundred, and still far above what a battery can afford to leave out." Make the same substitution in the advocate's "four orders of magnitude below" so the internal record does not preserve the bad figure.

findings.field: refutation, concession One ("Army artillery doctrine does not use the term"); also section 5 ("the claim has never proposed one")
findings.problem: The first sentence of the concession is correctly scoped — "not located in the text layer of the April 2016 edition ... searched here" — and the next sentence throws the scope away: "Army artillery doctrine does not use the term." That is a universal negative over an entire doctrinal corpus asserted from one document. I ran the project's own lint over this file in isolation: it scores 0 unscoped hits, and the reason is that "not located ... searched here" falls inside the regex's 160-character window and launders the sentence that follows. That is the documented failure mode verbatim — writers have learned the regex, not the rule — and a green ratchet is evidence about the fields it reads and nothing more. Section 5's "and the claim has never proposed one" is the same shape in a field the regex does not pattern-match at all.
findings.fix: "Army artillery doctrine does not use the term" -> "The 2016 manual searched here does not use the term anywhere in its text layer; it calls the thing rotation of the earth throughout, as does FM 6-40 in 1945." And "and the claim has never proposed one" -> "and none of the sources traced for this entry proposes one."

findings.problem: survives=4 obligates a concrete text change, and the preemptive instead describes changes as already present that are not in any rendered field. (a) It says "the entry says the tables are figure images and were not read" — that disclosure appears only in the module docstring; no reader-facing field (tldr, gloss, steelman, refutation, compression.note, straw_man) states it, and build.py strips advocate from the published data into review/advocate.json. The best_defense correspondingly has the defender saying "you did not read Table I — you said so", crediting us with an admission the page never makes. (b) It says the second move "must be answered in the body explicitly rather than by implication", but the NO ROTATION OF THE EARTH / NO WIND answer lives only in compression.note, which renders in a separate collapsed panel titled "The list overstates its own source" — a reader who opens the refutation and stops never meets it.
findings.fix: Add one sentence to the refutation after the parenthetical at the end of section 2: "The tables themselves are reproduced in the manual as figure images and were not read here; the figures above are computed from the standard expressions and cross-checked in section 3 against an independently published rifle figure, so if anyone reads the printed tables and the numbers disagree, this section is wrong." And move the standard-conditions answer into the body as a short section 5 lead-in: NO ROTATION OF THE EARTH sits in the same standard-conditions list as NO WIND and a 70F propellant temperature, and para 3-63 says actual conditions "will never equate to standard conditions" — a baseline is not a denial. Then rewrite the preemptive in the past tense once both land.

findings.problem: The entry names Dubay proof 158 as one of the three modern ancestors of items 108/227, but the body never answers it, and the body's §2 headline superficially confirms it. Proof 158 (verified verbatim in the Internet Archive djvu text) grants co-rotation arguendo and concludes 'Hot-air balloons would also be forced steadily faster Eastwards as they ascended through the ever increasing atmospheric speeds.' Our §2 then presents 'at mid-latitudes it is predominantly eastward' as the fact that points 'the wrong way for the claim'. A well-informed defender replies: 158 predicted eastward sweeping; you have just reported it as observed and called it a refutation. The actual answer exists in the entry but is never connected — §1's angular-momentum result is westward (-4.7 m/s), i.e. the opposite sign to 158's prediction, and in solid-body rotation a rising balloon gains linear speed but no motion relative to the ground beneath it.
findings.fix: Add two sentences to §2 (or the end of §1) naming proof 158: solid-body co-rotation means uniform angular velocity, so a balloon rising 39 km is carried east faster in absolute terms and not at all relative to the ground under it — 158 confuses absolute speed with relative displacement. Then state that the residual that does exist runs westward at 4.7 m/s by angular-momentum conservation, which is the wrong sign for 158, and that the observed eastward drift is thermal-wind, identifiable by its latitude structure and its hemispheric sign reversal rather than by altitude.

findings.problem: The gloss reports proof 22 as 'Baumgartner, after some two and a half hours of ascent over New Mexico, "2500 miles West into the Pacific Ocean"'. Dubay's text reads 'spending 3 hours ascending over New Mexico'. The 2.5 h is the real ascent time (Wikipedia: launch 09:30 MDT, jump 12:07/12:08 MDT), not his. The refutation compounds it: 'Dubay's figure of about 2,500 miles is the equatorial version of that speed (1,039 mph) run for two and a half hours' — a reverse-engineering contradicted by the source's own stated duration. On his three hours the natural reconstruction is 868 mph x 3 h = 2,604 miles at 33 degrees N, not 1,039 mph x 2.5 h.
findings.fix: In the gloss, quote his own figure: 'after three hours of ascent (his figure; the real ascent was about two and a half)'. In §1, replace the reconstruction with 'Dubay's 2,500 miles is his three hours run at roughly the co-rotation speed; at 33 degrees N and the actual 2.5 h ascent the same reasoning gives 2,169 miles.' Either way the argument is unaffected, and the source stops being misreported.

findings.field: refutation (§2, radiosonde paragraph) and sources[] radiosonde label
findings.problem: The cited Wikipedia radiosonde page says the opposite of what we imply. Its sentence is: '...there may be concern that this could introduce problems into the model initialization. However, this appears not to be so except perhaps locally in jet stream regions in the stratosphere.' We render this as drift 'far enough that the drifting position and time have to be handled in model initialisation, and the article naming that problem singles out jet stream regions as where it bites', and the sources[] label repeats it. We dropped a negation and three hedges ('perhaps', 'locally', 'in the stratosphere') in our own favour, against our own citation — the hedge rule violated on our side.
findings.fix: Keep the verbatim drift quote, which is correct and load-bearing, and drop the assimilation gloss: '...far enough that the same article notes it could in principle disturb model initialisation, though it reports the effect as showing up at most locally, in stratospheric jet-stream regions.' If the stronger claim about drift-aware assimilation is wanted, cite an NWP source that actually makes it.

findings.problem: Internal arithmetic contradiction, in the paragraph the entry itself flags as the one where the rebuttal usually goes wrong. Two sentences apart we write the 43 km lag is 'about one part in a hundred of what the argument requires' and then 'It is wrong by three orders of magnitude'. One part in a hundred is two orders. Reproduced: 42.6 km against 2,169 miles (3,490 km) is a factor of 82.7, i.e. just under two orders on any reading; 43 km against the docstring's own '~4,000 km' is a factor of 93. The docstring carries the same error ('three orders below the ~4,000 km the argument needs'). The overstatement runs in our favour and a defender gets to say we inflated our own margin tenfold and contradicted ourselves in the same paragraph.
findings.fix: Change 'It is wrong by three orders of magnitude' to 'It is wrong by a factor of about eighty' (or 'by nearly two orders of magnitude'), and correct the docstring line to 'two orders below the ~3,500 km the argument needs'.

findings.problem: The Rowbotham search is miscounted and misclassified. We publish: 'Searching the 1865 Earth Not a Globe ... for balloon returns six passages. Five are about the shape of the horizon from the car.' In Project Gutenberg #69892 the word occurs thirteen times (lines 424, 441, 444, 452, 468, 473, 483, 488, 491, 503, 510, 1793, 2900), and the passage at line 1793 is not about horizon shape at all: 'When a balloon sails from an observer without increasing or decreasing its altitude, it appears gradually to approach the horizon' — Rowbotham's perspective explanation of why the Sun appears to ascend and descend. The docstring states the count flatly ('the word "balloon" occurs six times'), so this is not a passages-versus-occurrences quibble. The missed passage is the one that would most strengthen §3: the tradition's founder grounds the same linear-perspective law our sun-angle answer uses, with a balloon.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: 'the word occurs thirteen times: ten in one section on the apparent concavity of the sea seen from the car, one in Rowbotham's perspective explanation of the setting Sun, and one inside a block quotation from the Literary Gazette of 1851.' Then use the perspective passage in section 3: Rowbotham himself explains apparent descent by linear perspective and illustrates it with a balloon, which is the same law that produces converging crepuscular and anticrepuscular rays.

findings.field: passage.gloss ('Nineteen miles a second is the orbit, not the spin') and compression.note (final paragraph)
findings.problem: The 'different target' genealogy claim is over-precise about a source that does not make the distinction. We assert Carpenter's balloon 'is aimed at the Earth's revolution around the Sun' and that ancestor and descendant 'are answering different motions'. Carpenter's own text welds the orbital magnitude to the rotational direction: proof 44 reads 'the Earth is said to move at the rate of nineteen miles in a second of time, "from west to east"', and proof 49 'revolving through space from west to east at the rate of nineteen miles in a second'. He is arguing against 'the motion of the Earth' undifferentiated, using a number that belongs to the orbit and a direction that belongs to the spin. On a project whose product is provenance, attributing a distinction to an author who visibly does not draw it is the wrong kind of tidy.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Carpenter's number is the orbital one — nineteen miles a second — but he attaches it to a west-to-east direction (proofs 44 and 49), so he is not separating revolution from rotation at all; the modern versions retarget the same picture at the daily spin specifically, at over a thousand miles an hour.' Same finding, no invented precision.

findings.problem: Unscoped absence claim in published prose: 'No physical account says either thing.' That is a claim about an entire literature made from reading two Dubay proofs, and it is the construction the standing rule bans. It sits in straw_man.detail, which the ratcheting test in tests/test_provenance.py does not scan (the loop reads tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note and the cluster note), and in a phrasing none of the _ABSENCE patterns match. This is exactly the batch-8 finding the test's own comment records: writers have learned the regex, not the rule.
findings.fix: Rescope to the texts actually consulted: 'Neither claim corresponds to anything in standard atmospheric dynamics as set out in the thermal-wind and angular-momentum treatments cited here' — or, more simply, state the positive: 'What atmospheric dynamics actually describes is a fluid in near-solid-body rotation with measured departures, and a density profile that falls off smoothly with no boundary to locate.'

findings.field: straw_man.detail ('a rigid co-rotating shell that nobody proposes')
findings.problem: The charge partly misreads its own quotation. Dubay's proof 23, read past the clause we quote, ends: 'It would be spinning around a centre point, therefore the air closer to the ground will always move slower than the air higher up.' That is not a rigid shell being attacked in ignorance — it is a correct statement of what rigid (solid-body) co-rotation implies for linear speed, and it is the premise proof 158 then runs with. Calling it 'a rigid co-rotating shell that nobody proposes' invites the reply that near-solid-body rotation is exactly the zeroth-order model we ourselves defend two paragraphs earlier, so the distinction we are drawing is one of degree (the winds), not of kind.
findings.fix: Narrow the charge to what it can carry: the strawman is 'perfect synchronization' and the abrupt boundary of proof 159, not the altitude-dependent linear speed, which is a correct consequence of the model. Add: 'His own next clause states that consequence correctly; the error is not there but in supposing that a faster absolute speed aloft means motion relative to the ground below.' That also sets up the proof-158 answer the body is missing.

findings.field: passage.locator, passage.gloss, straw_man.detail, compression.note, sources[0].label (and docstring §1-§3)
findings.problem: Every Volume I page citation is one page too low. Verified against the cited scan itself (archive.org item GallileoWasWrong) three ways: the printed folio in each page's footer, archive.org's leafNum-to-pageNumber map, and a rendered image of the page. Actual folios: the three-item geokinetic list containing 'The Sagnac effect used in laser gyroscopes...' is on p. 710 (cited as 709); 'Claims and Responses: Claim #1' with 'Implicitly denied...' is on p. 711 (cited as 710); 'No measurement of absolute or preferred rotation...' is on p. 712 (cited as 711); Sagnac points 15-16 are on p. 742 (cited as 741); the Michelson-Gale Claims and Responses with 'plane of radiation' is on p. 746 (cited as 745); the Eddington-via-Sciama gyrocompass footnote 615 is on p. 311 (cited as 310). A reader turning to p. 709 of the cited scan lands on chapter 11's footnotes. The quotations themselves are all verbatim-correct; only the locations are wrong, in about ten places, on a project whose product is provenance.
findings.fix: Shift every Vol. I page reference up by one: 709->710, 710->711, 711->712, 741->742, 745->746, 310->311. Note also that the Sagnac form Δt = 4Aω/c² is on p. 745 but the sin φ form and the latitude geometry are on p. 746, so the compression note's 'at p. 745, their own derivation ... is Δt = 4Aω sinφ/c²' should read p. 746. The Vol. II citations are correct as to edition and chapter (verified: 'Seventh edition, Volume II, Chapters 7 to 13', 2013, ch. 10 opening at p. 157), but the quoted sentences are on p. 158 and 'No measurement...' on p. 159, so the range is better given as 157-159.

findings.problem: The block attributes to the source a claim it does not make and that our own gloss shows it does not make. We write that the book's 'implicitly denied' remark 'misdescribes the state of the physics' because 'the alternative is not denied in the literature; it is computed in it.' But (a) the book's subject is the geokinetic argument, not the physics literature — its sentence is 'All the various effects noted above depend on the assumption that the inertial effects can only be caused by the Earth's rotation', which is a charge against the popular argument that our own refutation concedes in its opening paragraph; (b) on that same page the book itself cites the computation, 'Barbour and Bertotti proved that a large hollow sphere (representing the distant star fields) rotating around a small solid sphere inside ... produced exactly the same pattern of Coriolis and centrifugal forces', and the 2013 Vol. II contents list sections titled 'Brill and Cohen's Geocentrism', 'Lynden-Bell's Geocentrism' and 'Barbour and Bertotti's Geocentrism'; and (c) our own gloss four paragraphs earlier quotes Eddington denying exactly that alternative from inside the literature ('We do not believe that if the heavenly bodies were all annihilated it would upset the gyrocompass'). So the sentence is contradicted by the source, by the source's own bibliography, and by our own entry.
findings.fix: Drop 'That misdescribes the state of the physics. The alternative is not denied in the literature; it is computed in it.' Keep the part that survives and is the real point: the book cites the rotating-shell literature accurately, so what a stationary-Earth cosmology owes is not an acknowledgement that the equivalence exists but a dynamics for the rotating cosmos (ARG-R01). If a straw man is still to be identified here, identify the narrower one — that the response treats the Machian alternative as one the geokinetic side ignores, when Eddington's objection quoted in the book's own footnote 615 shows it was considered and rejected on grounds the book does not answer at this point.

findings.problem: render.py line 242 emits this field through e() = html.escape, and this is one of only two treatment files in the repo that write markup into it (every other _b6-_b11 file keeps it plain). Published output will read literally: '“the assumption...', '<em>Physical Review</em>', and '<a href="#ARG-R01">ARG-R01</a>'. The cross-link to ARG-R01 is dead and the paragraph looks broken.
findings.fix: Rewrite straw_man.detail as plain text with literal typographic characters — curly quotes, em dashes — and no tags, matching ARG-A03 and every other entry. Move the ARG-R01 pointer into the refutation (section 7 already links it) or write it as bare text.

findings.field: refutation, section 2 ('Two numbers, and they are the argument')
findings.problem: 'They are the two components of a single vector of fixed length, so sin²φ + cos²φ = 1 and their quadrature sum is the same 15.041° per hour at every latitude on Earth' does not follow from the two rates as displayed two paragraphs above, because the tilt rate carries a sin(azimuth) factor. sqrt((15 sinφ)² + (15 cosφ sin Az)²) = 15 only when |sin Az| = 1. For a gyro whose axis points north (Az = 0) the tilt rate is zero and the quadrature sum is 15 sinφ. The underlying vector claim is correct — the vertical and horizontal components of Ω are Ω sinφ and Ω cosφ and those do sum in quadrature to Ω — but the sentence identifies the horizontal component with the tilt rate, which is the component resolved against the rotor's own axis. advocate.preemptive (2) makes this the load the whole answer to the ether-vortex objection rests on, so it needs to be exactly right.
findings.fix: Say it about the field rather than the readings: 'The vertical and horizontal components of Ω are Ω sin φ and Ω cos φ, and those two sum in quadrature to the same 15.041°/hr everywhere. The drift rate reads the first directly; the tilt rate reads the second, reduced by sin (azimuth) because only the part of the horizontal component perpendicular to the rotor axis can torque it — set the axis east-west and the tilt rate is the horizontal component itself.'

findings.problem: The central theorem silently equates 'the local vertical' with the geometric normal to the plane. What a gyrocompass's pendulous mass or mercury ballistic actually responds to is apparent gravity — the plumb line. On a flat-earth model that keeps 'down' perpendicular to the plane, the two coincide and the theorem is airtight; on a model with a self-gravitating disc the plumb line tilts inward with radius and the angle to a fixed rotation axis does vary from place to place. The entry's advocate section anticipates the ether-vortex escape but not this one, and it is the escape a physically literate defender reaches for.
findings.fix: Name the assumption and close it in a sentence: the theorem is about the direction the plumb line points, which on any flat model where 'down' is perpendicular to the plane is one direction everywhere; a model in which the plumb line tilts with distance from the centre has bought curvature under another name — a surface whose apparent vertical swings through a right angle is a curved equipotential, its ocean surface follows that equipotential, and it still cannot reverse the Foucault sense across a boundary it does not have.

findings.problem: The side-by-side blockquote a reader judges the drift from carries only the hedged material (p. 710 statement of the opposing case, p. 712 'has not been disproven experimentally'), and the note's argument — 'A not-disproven is not a result' — reads as though the book stopped there. It did not: at p. 746 it states flatly that the free motion of the pendulum and of the Michelson-Gale ring define planes 'relative to the rotating heavens'. Our own gloss prints that sentence and says so. Quoting a source up to the disjunction in the very field built to display the drift is the hedge rule violated on our side, and it makes the drift look larger than the evidence shows.
findings.fix: Add the p. 746 sentence to source_wording, then state why force_upgraded survives it: the book's flat statement is about FREE instruments — a pendulum and a light ring — while item 229 asserts it of the gyrocompass, the one instrument built to be Earth-referenced. That is the drift, and it is stronger with the flat statement in view than without it.

findings.problem: One of the two surviving legs of the self-contradiction is asserted rather than defended, and the entry's own concession is the tool that removes it. Item 224 is four words — 'No rotation proof mechanical.' — and in the geocentric idiom it reads 'there is no mechanical proof that the EARTH rotates', which is exactly what the refutation's first paragraph concedes ('no gyroscopic instrument can tell you whether the Earth turns or the cosmos turns around it') and what section 7 repeats. On that reading 224 is consistent with 229, not a denial of it, and the contradiction rests on item 12 alone. The entry answers a different objection (instrument grade) and then asserts 'it is a straight disagreement about whether there is a daily relative rotation for a gyroscope to register at all' without showing that the four words force that reading.
findings.fix: Either drop 224 and rest the verdict on item 12, whose 'anomalies indicating no rotation' is a reading-level claim already shown reversed by the originator's own filmed 15°/hr at ARG-A07 — or keep 224 and disarm the escape explicitly: 'Read 224 as no proof that the Earth in particular turns and it is not a contradiction, it is this page's own concession — in which case the list has published as proof a claim its own item 229 renders non-discriminating. Read it as no mechanical rotation detected at all and it contradicts 229. The list gives no way to tell which, and neither reading leaves item 229 standing.'

findings.problem: Our headline quote stops one sentence early, and the omitted sentence is the source's answer to the reading our gloss builds on it. In the Vol. II scan the passage continues: "But when the heavens are postulated to be in motion, it is Dr. Nieto's equations that are deficient, not ours." The gloss says the conditional "gives the whole game away"; Selbrede's very next line pre-empts exactly that reading (the conditional is counterfactual in his model, and he turns it into an attack on his critics' equations). On a page whose whole thesis is that trimming a source changes it, a defender gets to say we trimmed his paragraph at the most convenient point. The substance is answered elsewhere in the body (the rotation rate is an input, section 1), but the answer is never attached to the sentence that provokes it.
findings.fix: The 60-word cap blocks extending the quote (47 + 19 = 66). Handle it in the gloss instead, which is our own prose: after "would fall if they stopped", add a clause naming the rejoinder and answering it — e.g. "Selbrede's next sentence turns the concession round — when the heavens are postulated to be in motion, he says, it is his critics' equations that are deficient, not his — and that is fair as far as it goes; the objection here is not that the conditional is false but that the rate of turning it makes everything depend on is an input, read off the rotating-globe solution and put in by hand."

findings.problem: The verification claim is stated more precisely than the book's own citations warrant, and more strongly than the research note allows. The refutation says every paper "exists, at the journal, volume and page range it gives"; the TLDR says "cited at the right journal, volume and pages". Checked against the scans: Grøn and Eriksen is given in full and exactly right (the essay itself, printed p. 632: "General Relativity and Gravitation, Volume 21, No. 2, 1989, pgs. 105-124"); but Orwig carries NO volume number anywhere I could find — Vol. I footnote 1168 and the Vol. I bibliography both read "Physical Review D, 1757-1763, 1978", and the essay names Orwig without a citation at all; Brill and Cohen at Vol. I footnote 1188 reads "Physical Review, 143, Issue 4, March 25, 1966, pp. 1012, 1014" — quote pages, not the article range 1011-1015; Thirring is given as "Physikalische Zeitschrift 19, 33, 1918", a start page rather than a range. Nothing the book prints is wrong, which is the point the paragraph is making and it survives — but we credit it with a bibliographic precision it does not have, and the docstring's own instruction was 'say so, at that strength and no higher'. The TLDR carries the strongest form of it and is what most readers see.
findings.fix: Refutation: "Every bibliographic detail the book prints for them checks out — journal, volume and year — and where it gives a page range (Grøn and Eriksen at 105-124, Orwig at 1757-1763) the range is right; Orwig's volume number the book omits, and the pages it cites inside Brill and Cohen and inside Grøn and Eriksen are quote locations we did not open the papers to confirm." TLDR: "...are real, and every journal, volume and year the book gives for them checks out."

findings.problem: The two texts the renderer puts side by side do not support the label attached to them. render.py prints list_phrasing ("Geostationary satellites fit rotating sky model.") above source_wording ("This motion of the firmament is evidenced ... by geosynchronous satellites ... the satellites would fall to the earth") and then the drift label. Against that pairing the list is not upgraded — it is weaker than the source, which asserts evidential force flatly while the item only says "fit". force_upgraded means a concession or permission re-used as a proof, and the permission that justifies the label is the p. 637 "by definition" thesis, which appears only inside the note. A reader who reads the block as rendered sees a label the visible evidence contradicts, on the project's flagship mechanism.
findings.fix: Put the licensing sentence into the field that renders: source_wording = "'This motion of the firmament is evidenced ... by geosynchronous satellites ...' (p. 648), and, as the essay's thesis: 'it is impossible to launch an attack on geocentricity on the basis of general relativity, by definition' (p. 637)." The note already explains the reasoning and already concedes the enum choice is contestable; this only makes the block's own evidence carry its own label.

findings.problem: The box answers "proof of a moving earth is proof general relativity is a myth" by saying the Earth's rotation relative to the local inertial frames "is measurable, frame-independent, and measured, by ring-laser gyroscopes and by the Foucault pendulum the essay itself discusses", and stops. Read strictly it is true — the relational quantity is agreed by both accounts — but it reads as an evidential claim, and it is deployed two boxes away from a passage in which the source claims the Sagnac effect and Coriolis forces as evidence FOR the firmament's rotation, and a refutation that concedes perfect dragging makes the two descriptions indistinguishable. The defender's reply writes itself: under perfect dragging the compass of inertia turns with the heavens, so that measurement is exactly what we predict too. This is the class of opening the docstring's own section 7 was written to avoid — winning on a point where the defender is right.
findings.fix: Add one clause and close the box on the narrow point it actually needs: "...measured, by ring-laser gyroscopes and by the Foucault pendulum the essay itself discusses. Both accounts predict that measurement and neither can claim it — what is measured is the relative rotation of the ground and the local compass of inertia, and the models differ only over which of the two to call at rest. The point here is narrower: establishing that relative rotation would leave general relativity exactly where it was, so the second sentence's threat is empty."

findings.field: refutation, section 5 "Their own horizon distances are sqrt(2Rh)" (scripts/_b11_B02.py:308,310; same claim in docstring note 7 at :113)
findings.problem: The 6-ft/3-mile pairing is called "the cleanest single check on this page" and Carpenter's figures are said to BE the sphere's formula. They equally reproduce the zetetic tradition's own law, which Rowbotham states quantitatively at p. 160 of the same enlarged-edition file the entry quotes, citing Mayhew's Wonders of Science p. 357: an object vanishes beyond "3000 times its own diameter". 6 ft x 3000 = 3.4 miles, against the sphere's 3.00 miles and Carpenter's "about three miles" - the two laws (sqrt(2Rh) and 3000h) cross at an eye height of about 1.4 m, so the check is made at the one height where the rival predictions agree. The closing sentence then says the perspective account "has no dependence on the observer's height whatever", which Carpenter contradicts in proof 6 - the proof quoted three lines above - with "if we merely ascend a hill such as Federal Hill, Baltimore, we may see twenty-five miles away", and which Rowbotham contradicts in his stated proposition 2 ("the further any two bodies ... are asunder, the further must they recede before they appear to converge to the same point"), the clause that makes the vanishing distance scale with the eye's height above the plane.
findings.fix: Demote the 3-mile datum and promote the 200-mile one. Replace with: "Proof 32 does not discriminate: six feet at three miles is sqrt(2Rh) to two significant figures, but it is also the zetetic rule Parallax quotes at p. 160 - an object invisible beyond 'three thousand times its own diameter' puts a six-foot object at 3.4 miles - and the two laws cross at about 1.4 m of eye height, which is where Carpenter is standing. Proof 6 is where they part. Their law is linear in height and the sphere's goes as its square root: at the 26,675 ft a 200-mile horizon requires, three thousand diameters gives a horizon some fifteen thousand miles away. Carpenter reports two hundred." Delete "has no dependence on the observer's height whatever" and write instead "makes the range grow in direct proportion to the height, not as its square root"; fix docstring note 7 to match.

findings.field: refutation section 2(a) (:282), steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim first reply (:260), gloss (:251), tldr (:203-204)
findings.problem: Our headline internal-contradiction argument - his optics exempt the axis his own tilt-to-contact procedure uses - is presented as an oversight of his, and the source's printed answer to exactly that charge is nowhere in the refutation or the steelman. In TANGENTIAL HORIZON at p. 202, describing the same procedure we quote, Rowbotham says the dip required to bring cross-hair and horizon together is "the angle A, T, S, to which must be added the collimation", and repeats "always A, T, S, plus collimation"; his reason follows at pp. 203-204, two sentences after the sentence we quote from p. 203: "the spider's web of which the cross hair is made is placed in the actual centre; hence, in an observation, the point absolutely opposite to it is not seen, but only some other point minutely distant from it". The gloss acknowledges the escape route but attributes it to the 1865 text only, so a reader of the edition we quote is told his answer lives somewhere else; the TLDR then states the exemption flat, without the hedge the gloss carries.
findings.fix: In section 2(a), after the exemption quotation, add: "He saw the objection. In the same section he writes that the dip measured this way is the geometric angle 'to which must be added the collimation', because the cross-hair itself occupies the centre, so 'the point absolutely opposite to it is not seen, but only some other point minutely distant from it' (enlarged ed., pp. 202-204). That answer is available to him, and it is why (c) below is written not to depend on (a): whatever residual the spider-line leaves is a fixed property of one instrument." In the gloss, change "He has an answer to this in the 1865 text" to "He has an answer to this in both editions - 1865 puts it as ... and the enlarged edition restates it at pp. 203-204 ...". Soften the TLDR to "the optical defect he describes acts off the axis, and his own procedure puts the horizon on it".

findings.problem: "Rowbotham's own 66 feet, converted at the 10-to-17-mile ranges his text names" attributes a distance range to the source that neither text contains. Experiment 7 names "a length of ten to twenty miles" and "Ten miles on each side"; Dubay proof 60 names "a clear, flat 10-20 miles". Seventeen appears nowhere in either (the only "17 miles" in the enlarged edition is a latitude discrepancy in an Australian survey). Because the angle is proportional to the half-trace, the range the texts do name gives about 2.2 to 4.3 arcminutes, not 2.5 to 4.3. On a page whose subject is what sources actually say, a number in quotation-adjacent position that the source does not carry is the error we exist to catch.
findings.fix: "And Rowbotham's own 66 feet, converted across the ten-to-twenty-mile traces both texts name, is between about 2.2 and 4.3 arcminutes."

findings.problem: "The strongest version of this argument is not in the 1849 pamphlet, which was not reached for this review" asserts an absence and concedes in the same clause that the text was never searched. This is the enforced rule verbatim - unreachable is not absent - and the pamphlet is not a safe bet to wave away: its own title is "A description of several experiments which prove that the surface of the sea is a perfect plane", so sea-horizon experiments are exactly what it advertises. The docstring (note 3) has the honest version, resting on Experiment 15's Brighton buildings postdating 1849 and calling that corroborating rather than decisive; the published sentence dropped the scope.
findings.fix: "The strongest version of this argument is not located in either text read here; the 16-page 1849 pamphlet was not reached for this review and has not been checked for it, though Experiment 15 is sited at buildings that postdate 1849."

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, "It reverses" (:262); same argument in refutation 2(c) (:286)
findings.problem: The reversal test is built on a definition of collimation - "a fixed angular offset between the line of sight and the instrument's mechanical axis" - that is the surveyor's error, not the one our own passage block quotes from the source three screens earlier: "a slight divergence of the rays of light from the axis of the eye, on passing through the several glasses of the theodolite", demonstrated with a magnifying glass and explicitly radial (outward from the centre, zero at the centre). A radially symmetric magnification effect is not obviously face-dependent, so as written the two-face argument answers a different error from the one Parallax proposes, and a defender who has read the lens paragraph will say so. The test does still bite - his residual offset is fixed in the instrument frame, so transiting flips it relative to gravity - but the text never makes that connection.
findings.fix: Add one clause: "His 'collimation' is not the surveyor's line-of-sight offset but a radial divergence through the glasses - yet the test still applies, because on his own account the observed point sits at a fixed small offset from the cross-hair, fixed in the instrument, so transiting the telescope carries it to the other side of the vertical and the two-face mean removes it. The dip does not move, because it is fixed by gravity and geometry."

findings.field: passage.gloss, "The witnesses he calls do not testify for a plane either" (:252)
findings.problem: "A plane does not look like a bowl" is asserted as self-evident against a source that argues the opposite at length on the same pages, and that our own quotation is drawn from. Two paragraphs before the balloon accounts Rowbotham writes that on a plane the sea "appears to rise up on all sides equally and to surround him like the walls of an immense amphitheatre. He seems to be in the centre of a large concavity"; immediately after them he explains the appearance with the tunnel analogy, the surface rising to the line of sight "in the same manner that the ceiling and the floor of a long room ... appear to approach each other". Producing the bowl from a plane by perspective is the whole point of his model, so our one-liner engages nothing and hands a defender the reply.
findings.fix: Replace "A plane does not look like a bowl." with: "He has a theory of why a plane would look like a bowl - the surface rising to the eye-line in every direction, as the floor and ceiling of a long room appear to converge - so these witnesses are not neutral testimony he collected but reports his perspective model was built to accommodate. What they do not report is a plane; what they report is an appearance, and an appearance is the quantity under dispute."

findings.problem: The report-up is false. scripts/works.py WRK-WINSHIP-1899 carries the correct record - title "Zetetic Cosmogony; or, Conclusive evidence...", imprint "By 'Rectangle' [pseud.]. 2nd ed., enl. Durban, Natal: T. L. Cullingworth. 192 pp.", url guides.loc.gov/flat-earth/books, note "First edition date not established" - and the generated data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json agrees.
