findings.field: clusters.py B02 record (scripts/clusters.py:325-328), which renders inside this entry via render.py's a["basis"]
findings.problem: render.py prints the cluster basis line twice inside this argument - once under the verdict chip and again as the Refutation section's summary - so the sentence a skim reader gets is "Dip of horizon is measurable with a theodolite and grows with altitude." That is precisely the objection this entry demonstrates Rowbotham anticipated, reproduced with his own theodolite, and answered with a lens-free instrument, so our summary line states our case in the form the source already rebutted. The same record carries year="1849", while everything the entry treats is shown to be in the 1865 book or the enlarged editions. The docstring flags both at 11(a) and 11(b) and correctly keeps them out of published prose, but the fix has not landed, and this is the failure pattern curmudgeon.md numbers 5.
findings.fix: Anchor on the key "B02" (never the originator= line, which is byte-identical across B02/B06/B07/D12) and set note="Rowbotham measured the theodolite dip himself and blamed the lenses - but his own optics exempt the axis his own method uses." and year="1865", originator_work="Earth Not a Globe (1865); the dip and levelled-board material is in the enlarged editions". Then delete or retire scripts/_b10_B02.py, which also defines ENTRY = {"B02": ...} and will trip the batch collision assert.

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, refutation section 3, sources[] label for USNO
findings.problem: The phrase quoted three times as the US Naval Observatory's — "a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes" — is not on the cited page. https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/RST_defs (fetched 2026-08-11) reads: "The 50-arcminute geometric depression of the Sun's center used for the computations is obtained by adding the average apparent radius of the Sun (16 arcminutes) to the average amount of atmospheric refraction at the horizon (34 arcminutes)." The quoted wording is Andrew Young's, on https://aty.sdsu.edu/explain/sunset_time.html — "the sum of an average radius of 16 minutes, and a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes" — a page this entry already cites for something else. The substance (a fixed 34′, published in advance, used worldwide) is fully supported by USNO; only the quotation is misattributed. On a provenance project a quoted string attributed to a source that does not contain it is the exact charge we level at the list, and it sits in the sources[] label a reader would click to check.
findings.fix: Either quote USNO in its own words — 90.8333 degrees, and "the average amount of atmospheric refraction at the horizon (34 arcminutes)" — or keep the phrase and attribute it correctly: "what Andrew Young calls 'a nominal horizontal refraction of 34 minutes'". Fix the sources[] label the same way.

findings.problem: An unscoped absence claim about the whole book, in three fields, where the body scopes it correctly. TLDR: "on the one magnitude his book supplies for it". Steelman: "It is never measured." Advocate: "the correction he substitutes has one magnitude in the whole book". The refutation says the scoped, defensible thing — "The one magnitude he supplies for it, in the chapters read for this entry" — and the entry read ch. II and the SPHERICAL EXCESS / TANGENTIAL HORIZON sections of a 430-page third edition, not the book. This is failure mode 1 in review/curmudgeon.md migrating into the fields the ratchet does not scan, and it is in the TLDR, which is read first.
findings.fix: TLDR: "…is, on the only magnitude the chapters read for this entry supply, about 240 times too small." Steelman: replace "It is never measured." with "No measurement of it is located in the chapters read for this entry." Advocate (d): "the correction he substitutes has one magnitude in the chapters read here".

findings.field: refutation section 5 ("The discrepancy he needs it to absorb is his own figure: 11 feet 8 inches of expected drop for the fig. 3 experiment at p. 35")
findings.problem: This misdescribes his position at the one place it names. In the fig. 3 experiment Rowbotham reports that no drop was seen and treats the absence as proof; he needs to absorb nothing there, so collimation is not offered against that 11 ft 8 in. The places he actually deploys instrumental "refraction, or … collimation" are the horizon dip (za16), the Ordnance Survey's spherical excess (za43, p. 263), and the 1870 Bedford Level result, where at za45 p. 272 he calls it "fully sufficient to explain the position of the disc at B, and the flag at C" — an observed offset of order five to six feet, not eleven feet eight. A well-informed defender gets a free hit here: "you sized my substitute against a discrepancy I never asked it to explain." The conclusion is robust across all three cases (factors of roughly 100 to 600), so only the pairing needs repair, not the arithmetic.
findings.fix: Anchor the comparison to a case he actually applies it to, or reframe the yardstick: "…about half an inch. For collimation to stand in for curvature at that range it has to be able to produce what curvature produces there — on his own figures, 11 feet 8 inches over six miles, and the several feet he calls it 'fully sufficient' to explain in the 1870 Bedford result at p. 272. His substitute is short by a factor of roughly 240 against the first and of order 100 against the second."

findings.field: verdict_challenge.reasoning (rendered on the page via render.py line 234)
findings.problem: "item 263, 'Mirage optical ducts.', asserts atmospheric ducting as a mechanism in its own right, four items after 221 charges that invoking it is illegitimate." Item 263 is forty-two items after item 221, not four (checked against scripts/corpus.py ITEMS and scripts/assign.py ASSIGN: 221 -> B07, 222 -> B04, 223 -> B06, 263 -> B13). It is a false statement about our own dataset in the field that argues for a verdict change, and it is the cheapest thing on the page for a critic to check.
findings.fix: "…in its own right, forty-two items further down the same list from the point where 221 charges that invoking it is illegitimate." Or drop the distance: the self-contradiction limb needs only that both items are on the one list.

findings.problem: The compression block runs Dubay's proof 71 as source wording for item 221 and then reasons from it — "Both sources hedge and the item does not… Four words on the list carry neither the concession, nor the experiment, nor the photograph the objection was about" — which asserts that item 221 descends from a proof about Joshua Nowicki's photograph. No derivation is shown, and the item is a general charge about method with no photograph in it. Against the identification: the word "refraction" does not occur anywhere in the 200 Proofs text reproduced at https://flatearth.ws/eric-dubay (searched 2026-08-11; the only hits on that page are site navigation), so proof 71 never uses the term the item turns on. The docstring is honest about this — "THE MODERN LINK IS DUBAY 200 PROOFS #71" — but the published note reads as provenance, and README's rule is that an attribution that will not verify is withdrawn to untraced rather than carried.
findings.fix: Demote the Dubay half from source to parallel: "The nearest modern form of the same charge is Dubay's proof 71, though item 221's descent from it is not traced here — and it hedges the same way: 'while these certainly do occur…'". Leave the drift_type computed on the Rowbotham comparison, which is documented.

findings.problem: The Dubay quotation is cut mid-sentence at "unlike a hazy illusory mirage" with a closing quote and no ellipsis, in both fields. The sentence continues: "…, and on a ball-Earth 25,000 miles in circumference should be 2,400 feet below the horizon" (verified verbatim at flatearth.ws/eric-dubay, 2026-08-11). Stopping at the concession and dropping the flat conclusion that finishes the same sentence is the hedge rule violated on our side — the pattern the brief names explicitly — and it inflates the hedge_dropped finding, because the compression block shows a reader a concessive source whose next eleven words are an unhedged assertion.
findings.fix: Close the quotation with the rest of the sentence in both places: "…unlike a hazy illusory mirage, and on a ball-Earth 25,000 miles in circumference should be 2,400 feet below the horizon." The concession still stands, and the drift finding survives on the four-word item carrying neither half.

findings.problem: "within a single British survey the predicted lean between stations is a matter of arcseconds and is swamped by exactly the local effects that produced Rowbotham's anomaly" is false, and it contradicts our own refutation. The table's stations are Dunnose (50 deg 37' 08") to Clifton (53 deg 27' 31"): the two verticals lean by 2.84 deg, about 10,200 arcseconds. Dunnose to Greenwich alone is 51' 32" = 3,092 arcseconds. That lean is not a small effect swamped by local ones; it IS the astronomical latitude difference the survey measured, and the 2-4" station deflections perturb it at the 0.2% level - which is exactly what refutation section 3 says two paragraphs earlier. As written, the block makes Rowbotham's inference look reasonable at British scale and hands a critic a self-contradiction inside one entry.
findings.fix: Replace with the true reason the widening matters: within the survey the lean between stations is degrees, and it is the very quantity Rowbotham's table records as latitude - his own evidence presupposes it. The item's "worldwide" then adds the scale at which two verticals differ by up to 180 degrees and bridge towers are built non-parallel on purpose. Do not describe the British-scale lean as arcseconds; that number belongs to the deflection of the vertical, not to the lean.

findings.problem: Sensors 16(4):565 (2016) is credited to "Barzaghi et al." The paper is real and the title, journal, volume, issue and year are all correct, but its authors are Luca Vittuari, Maria Alessandra Tini, Pierguido Sarti, Eugenio Serantoni, Alessandra Borghi, Monia Negusini and Sebastien Guillaume (verified at mdpi.com/1424-8220/16/4/565). Barzaghi is not among them; the slip is most likely from the ITALGEO geoid model the paper uses. A misattributed citation in a published source list is the worst available error on a site whose product is provenance.
findings.fix: Relabel as "Vittuari et al., 'A Comparative Study of the Applied Methods for Estimating Deflection of the Vertical in Terrestrial Geodetic Measurements', Sensors 16(4):565 (2016)".

findings.problem: "on its shortest arc, Dunnose to Greenwich at about 0.86 deg" - Dunnose-Greenwich is the second shortest arc in Rowbotham's table, not the shortest. Solving the table's own mean-latitude column gives Clifton 53 deg 27' 31", Greenwich 51 deg 28' 40", Arbury Hill 52 deg 13' 28", Dunnose 50 deg 37' 08" (each cross-checks against the published station latitudes). Arbury Hill-Greenwich is 44' 48" = 0.747 deg; Dunnose-Greenwich is 51' 32" = 0.859 deg. A defender who opens the table catches this in a minute, and the whole magnitude argument turns on picking the most sensitive arc.
findings.fix: Name Arbury Hill to Greenwich, 0.747 deg = 2,688 arcseconds, and recompute: 0.20% of that is 5.4 arcseconds of latitude error - still squarely inside the Britannica's range, and a stronger version of the same point.

findings.problem: Both quoted quantities from the Sensors paper are attached to the wrong referents. "The first two agree 'well within the 1 arcsec level'" - the paper's phrase describes the standard deviations of the GNSS-plus-levelling method alone ("The method that combines leveling and GNSS has slightly larger standard deviations; although well within the 1 arcsec level, which was assumed as threshold"), not the agreement between two methods. And "the gravity-derived values sit about 2.5 arcseconds out" turns a standard deviation into an offset: the paper says "the geoid model based method, whose 2.5 arcsec standard deviations exceed this threshold, is also statistically consistent with the others". The docstring gets this right; the prose does not.
findings.fix: Quote the sentence that actually supports the claim - "The three methods are in excellent agreement, with an operational supremacy of the astro-geodetic method" - and describe the 1 arcsec and 2.5 arcsec figures as each method's precision, with the geoid model "statistically consistent with the others" despite exceeding the 1 arcsec threshold.

findings.problem: The entry states as established history that the British arc anomaly was caused by deflection of the vertical: "traces to the plumb line being pulled sideways", "The explanation, when it came, was...", "its cause is the thing he was arguing against", "The arcs disagreed because...". The 1911 Britannica article we cite does not say this. It gives station deflections for the English survey and the "perplexity" remark, but its discussion of a prolate result is about the French Cassini arc, not the English one, and it presents the English survey as successful work. Our own docstring note 6 warns: "State this as a magnitude argument, NOT as a published reanalysis of that table - we did not find one." The published prose does the thing the note forbids, in four places including the TLDR.
findings.fix: Keep the magnitude argument and drop the causal verbs: the spread in his table is 0.20%, which on his most sensitive arc is about 5 arcseconds of latitude - the ordinary size of the station deflections the Britannica computed for that same survey. Say that no reanalysis of Rowbotham's specific table was located, so this is a consistency argument rather than a published attribution. In the TLDR, "is the size of" instead of "traces to".

findings.field: refutation section 2, horn 2 (line 261); docstring note 5 (line 88); advocate.preemptive (line 332)
findings.problem: "set out six pages earlier in the same chapter" is wrong by roughly a factor of two. In the same sacred-texts transcription the entry paginates by, the plumb-lines passage sits on printed p. 245, DECLINATION OF THE POLE STAR immediately precedes THE "DIP SECTOR" which begins at p. 232, so the perspective account is about fourteen printed pages earlier (on the reformatted archive.org scan the gap is nine to ten pages, not six either). The section, chapter and the quoted phrase "an ordinary effect of perspective" all check out - only the distance is wrong, and preemptive expressly tells the reader to go and check it.
findings.fix: "set out earlier in the same chapter, under the heading 'Declination of the Pole Star' at pp. 230-231" - or simply cite the heading and drop the page count.

findings.problem: Two printed-page citations each run one page long against the pagination they name. The quoted passage lies entirely between the [p. 245] and [p. 246] markers on sacred-texts za40.htm - it is on p. 245, not "pp. 245-246". The von Gumpach extract is cited at "pp. 243-244", but "without any proof or reason whatever" and "such imaginary directions as are needed" both fall before the [p. 243] marker (i.e. on p. 242), and "unsupported by even the shadow of a reason" is on p. 243; nothing quoted is on p. 244. Related: straw_man attaches "without any proof or reason whatever" to the assumption that the plumb line is normal to the local horizon, but in the source that phrase governs astronomy's assumption that plumb lines do NOT all meet at the centre; the "shadow of a reason" phrase is the one about the tangent plane.
findings.fix: "printed p. 245" in the locator and the source label; "pp. 242-243" in straw_man.detail; and split the two von Gumpach charges rather than merging them - he says astronomy assumes without proof that the plumb lines do not converge on the centre, and separately that their perpendicularity to the tangent plane is unsupported by even the shadow of a reason.

findings.problem: Murray's "It has been found impossible to explain the want of agreement in a satisfactory way" is attached to the wrong discrepancy. In both the 1865 and 1881 texts that sentence refers to the mismatch between the polar/equatorial axis ratio derived from the Beachy Head-Dunnose degree perpendicular to the meridian and that from meridional degrees, and it comes BEFORE the table. The "oblong instead of an oblate spheroid" remark about the degrees decreasing comes after it. We present the concession as Murray admitting the table's northward decrease could not be explained ("his source concedes it could not be satisfactorily explained").
findings.fix: Attribute each remark to its own referent: Murray reports that the perpendicular-degree and meridional-degree results disagreed and that the disagreement could not be explained satisfactorily, AND separately that the tabulated degrees appear to decrease as if the Earth were oblong. Both are real, and keeping them apart costs one clause.

findings.problem: The advocate is rated 4, which the project's own rubric says must be answered in the body, and the fourth move - Tamarack, the only real side-by-side plumb-line experiment anyone can point at - is answered nowhere a reader can reach. render.py renders tldr, passage, steelman, refutation, compression, straw_man and verdict_challenge; it does not render advocate. So the preemptive's "That paragraph should be added to the body if this argument is ever attacked in public" parks the answer in an unpublished field, in the future tense. Refutation section 5 also asserts that neither text observed a plumb line, which invites the reader to ask whether anyone ever did.
findings.fix: Move the Tamarack arithmetic into the body as a short paragraph at the end of section 1 or 5: 15 ft of separation over 4,250 ft of depth predicts 0.0031 ft (about 0.9 mm) of convergence; McNair's results across the shafts ran -0.028 to +0.141 ft with error under 0.003 ft, so the apparatus could not have detected the effect in either direction - a statement about the shaft, not about the men. All of it is verified against Simanek's account (Science XV, 20 June 1902).

findings.problem: The through-line that 'Constant solar diameter' is Proctor's sentence, borrowed — TLDR: 'the words are a quotation from the astronomer he was arguing against'; §3 heading: 'is Proctor's sentence, borrowed'; compression.note: 'Nothing was misquoted; the speech act moved' — understates Carpenter's own commitment and mislocates the drift. findings.problem: "the 4/3 factor is the standard-atmosphere case, a duct is a larger k, and a sub-refractive layer is a smaller one." Sub-refraction is correctly a smaller k, but a duct is not "a larger k": in the standard treatment k = 1/(1 + a dn/dh), superrefraction is k > 4/3, and ducting begins at dN/dh = -157 N/km, exactly where k passes through infinity (the ray follows the Earth's curvature) and then goes negative. That is the point where the effective-earth-radius model degenerates and engineering practice switches to modified refractivity and parabolic-equation solvers. An RF engineer will spot this in the one paragraph the entry offers as "the honest qualification" — and the correct version is STRONGER for us, because modified refractivity is M = N + 0.157h and 0.157 per metre is 10^6/R: the standard ducting formalism is an earth-flattening transformation whose flattening term is proportional to 1/R, which is precisely the §5 thesis.
findings.fix: Replace with: superrefraction is a larger k; a duct is the limit at which the effective-radius model itself breaks, and the standard treatment beyond it is modified refractivity M = N + 0.157h — an earth-flattening transformation whose 0.157 per metre is 10^6/R. Then the ducting concession lands on the same 1/R structure as the rest of the entry.

findings.field: refutation, second paragraph ("Second, the ledger, and it is Rowbotham's") + tldr, second sentence
findings.problem: The ledger — the entry's central positive claim, repeated in the closing verdict paragraph and paraphrased in the TLDR — counts Rowbotham's chapter titles rather than his chapters, and counts the two sides on different scales. (1) We say the contents page assigns "a separate chapter, and a separate mechanism" to "the cause of day and night and the seasons (VI)". Rowbotham's Section 6 says the opposite in its own words: "Thus, day and night, long and short days, Winter and Summer, the long periods of alternate light and darkness at the pole, arise simply from the Sun's position in relation to the north pole" — i.e. VI is derived from IV and V, exactly the move we credit the globe with. It is not an independent stipulation, so "six stipulations against two" is five at best. (2) The same paragraph lists XIII among costs "still to be paid for separately", but Section 13 runs on the same convergence-of-parallels principle as Section 7 ("horizontal lines parallel to each other appear to approach or converge in the distance") — one principle, two applications. (3) XII is a miscellanea chapter ("Moon's Phases--Moon's appearance--Planet Neptune--Pendulum Experiments"), not a chapter assigned to the phases. (4) On the other side of the ledger, "a tilted Earth turning once a day while it goes round the Sun" is three independent stipulated inputs (rotation, obliquity, orbital revolution) counted as one. Under a symmetric count the six explananda cost the plane five and the globe three — still our way, but nothing like six against two. This is precisely the "metric wearing a lab coat" objection our own advocate block raises, and the sharpest version of it is available in the source text we quote elsewhere in the same entry, so a defender does not even have to leave our page to make it.
findings.fix: Rewrite the paragraph as a symmetric count and drop the number "six". Concede VI outright in one clause — "Rowbotham derives day and night and the seasons from IV and V himself: 'Thus, day and night, long and short days, Winter and Summer ... arise simply from the Sun's position in relation to the north pole' (Section 6) — so that one is his derivation, not his stipulation" — and then count what is genuinely stipulated on each side: on the plane, that the Sun circles daily over it (IV), that the circle's diameter varies annually with nothing to set it (V), that parallels converge at a finite vanishing point (VII, reused at XIII), a dark body for lunar eclipses (IX), and a phase mechanism for the Moon (XII); on the globe, daily rotation, axial tilt, and annual orbit, from which all six follow. Five against three, named on both sides. Then say what actually carries the weight, which is not the ratio: the plane still owes Section VIII, the southern sky, and the eclipse mechanism, and those are unpaid rather than merely numerous. In the TLDR, "gives sunrise, the seasons and the Sun's changing path a separate mechanism each" must go — in the source the seasons and the changing path are one mechanism; replace with "gives sunrise, the eclipses and the Sun's annually changing path a separate mechanism each, where a tilted Earth turning as it orbits delivers all of them from three."

findings.field: tldr, third sentence + refutation, fourth paragraph ("Fourth, the historical inversion") + sources[5] label
findings.problem: The historical-inversion headline — the entry's docstring calls it "THE HEADLINE" and says it is "DOCUMENTED IN TWO TRANSLATIONS" — rests on a construal that only one of the two translations supports, and we tell the reader they agree. The TLDR asserts flatly that "Ptolemy had already called the rotating-Earth account 'this simpler conjecture'", and the body says "Simpler is Ptolemy's word for his opponents' account, granted to them", offering Toomer as corroboration: "Toomer's independent rendering says the same thing." It does not say the same thing on the one word the claim needs. The unattributed CCSU text (Taliaferro's rendering) attaches the adjective to the hypothesis — "in accordance with this simpler conjecture"; Toomer, the standard scholarly translation and the one credited in MPRL footnote 32, attaches it to the mode of argument — "at least from simpler considerations", which reads as a concession about the level of analysis, not about the economy of the rival model. Both render the same Greek (kata ge to haplousteron), which is neuter and adverbial and genuinely bears Toomer's reading. So our own second citation, presented in the sources list as "an independent check on the wording", is the one that does not check the wording. A classicist or a well-informed defender will find this in one move, and it lands in the TLDR.
findings.fix: Stop claiming agreement on the operative word, and keep the part both renderings do support, which is all the argument needs. In the body: "Toomer, the standard modern translation, renders the same Greek differently where it matters — 'there is perhaps nothing in the celestial phenomena which would count against that hypothesis, at least from simpler considerations' — attaching 'simpler' to the level of argument rather than to the hypothesis. On either rendering the concession is the same and it is the concession that matters: Ptolemy grants the rotating Earth the appearances of the stars and rejects it on terrestrial physics, clouds and projectiles left behind by a turning Earth." In the TLDR, drop the direct attribution of the phrase to Ptolemy: "Ptolemy had already granted the rotating-Earth account the appearances of the stars and rejected it on terrestrial physics instead." And change the sources[5] label from "an independent check on the wording" to "the standard scholarly rendering, which differs from the CCSU text on where 'simpler' attaches".

findings.problem: The advocate block misses the sharpest move available, and the miss is created by our own first paragraph. We open by conceding that parsimony's first legitimate job is to "break ties between rivals that predict the same observations" — which is precisely what the geocentric branch claims its position is, on general covariance (ARG-R01). A defender turns our sentence around: by our own statement of the rule, this is not an illegitimate use of parsimony at all, it is the licensed one, and the burden shifts to us to show the rivals are not empirically equivalent. The body does answer it, but only at the very end and implicitly (aberration, parallax, ring laser, barycentric correction), and the advocate block — which is where we are supposed to have found this first — does not raise it.

That is our claim about this case, so you have licensed the argument and then complained about it"), and close the door in the first paragraph of the refutation with one clause: "— and the tie-breaking job only arises once the rivals are shown to predict the same observations, which is the question aberration, parallax and the ring laser settle before parsimony is reached."

findings.problem: The TLDR opens "Simplicity is a preference, not a measurement" — which is the SURFACE bust the entry's own steelman labels "weak — do not use" and says "loses immediately", on the ground that parsimony is Newton's first Rule of Reasoning and is formalised in model selection "where the penalty on free parameters is derived rather than asserted". findings.field: untraceable (Sargent paragraph) + sources[Flat Earth Society interview]
findings.problem: The Flat Earth Society interview we cite and quote does contain the word we say is not located in it. Sargent: "But on a flat earth model, well it could also be density. I think its electromagnetic. I think its a molecular magnet that pulls things down." That is about gravity, not the dome, so our sentence — "an electromagnetic, toroidal or resonance description of IT is not located in either" — is narrowly true. But it is the single best quote-mine available against this entry, in a source we link, and a defender needs one sentence to make the page look like it searched carelessly. Worse for a provenance review: this is the strongest proximate lead for item 201's exact phrasing. A distributor reading this one page meets "an enclosed system with a dome over it" and "I think its electromagnetic" four paragraphs apart, and "Firmament as electromagnetic dome." is what that fusion would look like. We found the lead, read past it, and published the negative.
findings.fix: Add to the Sargent paragraph, before "The video series itself was not reached": "One qualification, because a reader who opens the interview will find it. Sargent does use the word electromagnetic there — but of the downward pull, not of the dome: asked about gravity he answers “I think its electromagnetic. I think its a molecular magnet that pulls things down.” The dome, a few paragraphs earlier, is Genesis 1:6 and the planetarium. So the two nouns of item 201 are both on that page and the sentence joining them is not — which is a lead we record rather than a source we can credit." Stating it strengthens the untraced finding instead of leaving it as a hole; do not withdraw the untraced verdict on the strength of it.

findings.problem: The entry's own advocate rates the 10.59-versus-7.83 gap as the defender's strongest move (move two, survives=4) and preemptive (a) requires that we state it in our own voice up front. The refutation does. The two fields that render BEFORE it do not. The TLDR says "Schumann derived the mode ladder in 1952 from a sphere of radius 6,371 km, and Balser and Wagner measured it from 1960" — derived, then measured, with nothing between them; and steelman.why says "A prediction made from an assumed shape, before the measurement, is the strongest evidence about shape that this phenomenon can carry, and it did not come out flat." As stated, that prediction failed by 26%. A reader meets the unqualified prediction-then-measurement story twice (tldr first of all, steelman as section 2) before meeting "the absolute number does not settle anything" in section 3. That is the TLDR outrunning the body, and the steelman outrunning it in the same direction.
findings.fix: TLDR, replace the middle sentence with: "Schumann derived the mode ladder in 1952 from a sphere of radius 6,371 km, and Balser and Wagner measured it from 1960 — the ideal formula overshoots the fundamental by a quarter, for a known reason, but the ratios between the modes, which contain no cavity size at all, come out spherical to a few per cent." In steelman.why, after "strongest evidence about shape that this phenomenon can carry", insert "— and it is the mode ratios that carry it, not the absolute frequency, which the ideal formula misses by 26% for reasons set out below —" before "and it did not come out flat."

findings.problem: The range does not reproduce from the two ladders printed three lines above it, under either convention. Disc 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65 against observed 1, 1.80, 2.59, 3.36, 4.15 gives deficits of 11.7%, 17.4%, 31.5%, 36.1% relative to observed, or excesses of 13.2%, 21.0%, 46.1%, 56.6% relative to the disc. findings.problem: A "the one" quantifier contradicted by the source cited for the sentence around it. The Wikipedia Schumann resonances article's extraterrestrial section reports, for Mars, "radio emission spectra that have been associated with Schumann resonances", and treats the Venera lander data as the strongest evidence for Venus. findings.field: tldr and verdict_challenge.reasoning (item 202, technical reading only)
findings.problem: advocate.preemptive (d) states the rule for this entry: both readings of "toroidal", technical first and iron-filings second, "because answering only the technical one is the straw man the defender is accusing us of". The refutation §4 obeys it. The two summary fields do not. The TLDR answers 202 purely on the technical reading, and verdict_challenge.reasoning rests 202's self-contradiction entirely on it — "the component that geomagnetism says is confined to the core". That leaves the challenge resting on a definition the item's author was almost certainly not using, when the loose reading has its own self-contradiction sitting in our refutation unused and arguably stronger: the doughnut a compass responds to is described by the IGRF as a spherical-harmonic expansion truncated at degree 13, generated in a convecting liquid outer core whose depth was fixed by seismic waves travelling through a ball.
findings.fix: In verdict_challenge.reasoning, after "not detectible at the surface", add: "and on the looser reading the item is more likely to intend — the iron-filings doughnut — the same thing happens one level down: that field is described by the IGRF as a spherical-harmonic expansion and generated in a spherical convecting outer core mapped by seismology, so the geometry is inside the citation on either reading." In the TLDR, "the toroidal part of the field is the part confined to the core and not measurable at the surface at all" → "the toroidal part of the field is the part confined to the core and not measurable at the surface at all — and the part a compass does feel is mapped, since Gauss, as a spherical harmonic series."

findings.problem: "The same resonance shows up in diurnal Earth tides recorded by superconducting gravimeters — instruments in basements, weighing the local pull of gravity, with no astronomical input at all." That is false about the method actually cited, and it is the exact overclaim our own advocate/preemptive forbids. Rosat & Lambert (2009), which I read in full (hal.science/hal-00643157/file/11489.pdf), invert complex tidal gravimetric factors for the diurnal lunisolar waves (Ψ1, Φ1 are named as the ones closest to the resonance), computed with ETERNA against an astronomically derived tidal potential and corrected for ocean loading with FES2004 — the forcing, the wave frequencies and the reference amplitudes are all astronomical. The −430-day figure is a celestial-frame period converted from a nearly-diurnal terrestrial-frame resonance using the Earth's rotation rate, so it is not innocent of the assumption at issue either. Our advocate's move 2 attacks precisely this ("agreement between two analyses that share that theory and its tidal model") and our preemptive answers "never write that the gravimeters independently confirm the core" — yet the very next sentence of the published body writes that the resonance is "independently visible in a gravimeter in Germany". The safe version sits in review/advocate.json, which build.py strips from the published data; the unsafe version is what renders.
findings.fix: Replace with: "…recorded by superconducting gravimeters — instruments in basements that weigh the local pull of gravity and never observe a star, though the resonance is extracted from the lunisolar diurnal tides and so is not free of astronomical modelling." Then narrow the closing sentence to the load-bearing claim the preemptive already identified: the resonance is parameterised by the core–mantle boundary flattening, so a moving-heavens account has to explain why the sky is tuned to the Earth's interior. Also correct "a gravimeter in Germany": the paper inverts 15 GGP stations worldwide (Boulder, Bad-Homburg, Cantley, Canberra, Esashi, Matsushiro, Moxa, Membach, Medicina, Metsähovi, Potsdam, Strasbourg, Vienna, Wettzell, Wuhan) expressly "to minimize local effects" — the true version is stronger than the invented specific.

findings.field: refutation §2, passage.gloss, sources[12].label — printed page numbers in Galileo Was Wrong 7th ed.

Using the Internet Archive leaf→folio map (…_page_numbers.json) and the item's search-inside index: "carries the stars with it" is on leaf 243 = printed p. 230, not p. 229 (leaf 242 = 229 holds the two Eddington footnotes); "the highest angular resolutions can be achieved by interferometry" / "On Telescope Limits" is on leaf 1055 = printed p. 249, not Vol. II p. 248; the word "Gaia" is on leaf 259 = printed p. 246, not p. 245 (the sentence starts on 245 with "…such as the ESA"). Docstring notes 5, 6 and 7d carry the same numbers and should move with them.

findings.field: passage.gloss, paragraph 2 ("The claim is a circularity charge…")
findings.problem: "The conclusion is stated flatly and without qualification, and there is no hedge here to shelter behind" is immediately followed by the quotation that refutes it: "Without this methodology, all VLBI measurements are invalid to prove whether the Earth is rotating." The sentence opens with an express condition. A defender's cheapest reply is to point at our own block quote. Worse, the qualification is the best thing in the passage for us and we are throwing it away: the antecedent is the multi-source methodology, which is standard practice and has been since 1979, so on the source's own terms the conclusion never triggers. The hedge rule's whole subject is representing a source's strength accurately, and this is the one place in the entry where we get it wrong — in the source's favour rhetorically, against our own interest argumentatively.
findings.fix: "The conclusion is stated as fact rather than as a possibility, and it is general — 'all VLBI measurements' — but it carries one condition, and the condition is the entry's opening: 'Without this methodology, all VLBI measurements are invalid to prove whether the Earth is rotating.' The methodology in question is ordinary geodetic practice, so the antecedent fails and the conclusion lapses on the book's own terms."

findings.problem: "…but the objection's factual premises fail, including the one about poor resolution". The bare plural reads as universal, and the body's first move is a concession that one of the objection's factual premises is correct: the Tōhoku figures really were computed rather than measured, and JPL's own release says the computed change is smaller than the accuracy with which the length of day can be measured. The TLDR erases the concession that is the refutation's strongest credibility move and asserts a quantifier the body denies in its opening paragraph. This is recurring failure #2/#6 exactly.
findings.fix: "…but the objection's premises about the instrument fail — the single source, the poor resolution, the unchanged historical record — including the one about resolution: …". That keeps the punch, matches §7's own enumeration, and leaves the conceded premise standing where the body puts it.

findings.field: passage.gloss, paragraph 6 ("An internal tension worth knowing about")
findings.problem: "…and thereby states the principle — resolution goes as wavelength divided by baseline — that makes the ch. 2 objection wrong." The book states no such principle there. I read the whole "On Telescope Limits" section in the OCR (leaf 1055): the words baseline, wavelength and aperture do not occur in it. It says only that point sources closer than the angular resolution cannot be resolved, that a single optical telescope does worse than one arcsecond in practice, that "the highest angular resolutions can be achieved by interferometry", and gives VLTI 0.001″ and Hubble 0.05″. Both examples are optical, so a defender reconciles the two chapters in one line — "we said radio wavelengths give poor resolution; the VLTI is an optical instrument, there is no contradiction" — and our claimed tension evaporates. The real tension is narrower and survives that reply: ch. 2 treats resolution as a function of wavelength alone, while ch. 10 concedes that interferometry, not aperture, sets the achievable resolution.
findings.fix: "…gives the Very Large Telescope Interferometer's target of 0.001 arcseconds and Hubble's 0.05 arcseconds — conceding that it is interferometry rather than aperture size that sets the achievable resolution, which is the variable the ch. 2 objection leaves out. (Both of the book's examples are optical; the physics that closes the gap for radio is in section 3 below.)"

findings.problem: "The imputed reasoning — that a belief in rotation is what makes the shortcut seem acceptable — is supplied by the paragraph, not by anything in the analysts' documentation." That is an unscoped absence claim about an entire corpus (NASA/JPL/IVS/IERS documentation) that nothing in this entry records having searched. straw_man.detail is reader-facing (render.py line 242) but is NOT one of the six fields the ratchet in tests/test_provenance.py scans (tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note, cluster note), so the counter stays green — this is literally the batch-8 finding that the construction migrates into unscanned fields, one batch later.
findings.fix: "…is supplied by the paragraph; it is not stated in the description of the analysis the frame is actually built from (Charlot et al. 2020, Sects. 2–3), which is the document searched for this entry."

findings.problem: The quotation "excellent agreement with the independent measurements by VLBI" could not be verified in any accessible copy. Schreiber et al., PRL 107:173904 (2011) is closed access (OpenAlex reports no repository full text anywhere; APS returns 403; no arXiv version located). Crossref confirms title, five authors, volume and article number, and the PubMed abstract confirms the 16 m² helium-neon ring laser, the Wettzell affiliation and direct detection of the Chandler and annual wobble — but it says the detection "is verified by comparing the time series of the ring laser measurements against the 'C04 series' of Earth rotation data from the International Earth Rotation and Reference System Service." IERS C04 polar motion is a multi-technique combination in which GNSS, not VLBI, dominates. So both the quoted phrase and the sentence built on it — "reproduces polar motion derived from quasars" — rest on text I cannot reach and may misdescribe the comparison series. The flicker-floor figure and the Apr–Jul 2010 window are unverified for the same reason.
findings.fix: Either cite the page of the PRL where that phrase appears, or fall back to what the abstract carries: "…detected the Chandler and annual wobbles directly, verified against the IERS C04 Earth-rotation series." And soften "polar motion derived from quasars" to "the same polar motion the space-geodetic services measure", unless the VLBI-specific comparison can be confirmed in the paper.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py, cluster "E15" (name and note) — reported up, not editable from this file
findings.problem: The cluster line that renders beside the verdict chip contradicts the entry beneath it. name="VLBI, interferometry and Gaia reductions assume an Earth frame" and note="Same convenience-frame error as R08", while the gloss states in terms: "The claim is a circularity charge, not a frame-convention point", and the located source argues something stronger — that VLBI presupposes rotation and reads one source at a time, so it cannot demonstrate rotation. findings.problem: The section headed "The dates are predicted, years out, in a heliocentric frame" opens "This is where the argument is decided, because prediction is the one thing a coordinate relabelling cannot manufacture" and closes "Every one of those predictions is an assertion about where the Earth will be, and how fast, on a given night. They are not compatible with the Earth being somewhere else." §5 (line 230) then states the opposite in our own voice: a Tychonic arrangement "reproduces every radiant, every closing speed, every apex asymmetry and every annual date, because it is the same geometry with the labels moved" — i.e. the relabelling DOES manufacture the predictions, and under it the Earth is not anywhere else, it is fixed, and the predictions still land. compression.note repeats the concession ("no meteor observation discriminates"). The entry's own advocate.preemptive forbids exactly this move, and build.py strips the advocate block from the published corpus, so the instruction is invisible to readers while the violated sentence is not. This is the defender's first move and our advocate names it in the first line of best_defense.
findings.fix: Replace line 204 with a claim the page can keep: "This is where the model earns its keep, because a prediction registered in advance is a test the bookkeeping can fail." Replace line 212 with: "Every one of those predictions is an assertion about the geometry of an encounter — where the Earth and the stream will be relative to each other, and how fast, on a given night. That geometry is what a relabelling preserves and what a wrong model gets wrong; the predictions test the geometry, not the choice of origin, and section 5 says which of those the list needs."

findings.problem: "the observed peak, radiant, rate and width in general agreement with the models". The rate did not agree with the cited predictions and our own docstring note 5 says so in terms: "It reached only ~1/50 of storm level (Ye & Vaubaillon 2022) — quote the timing, not the rate." Ye & Vaubaillon (cited in our sources) state "Increased activity of the τ-Herculid meteor shower has been observed on 2022 May 30–31 but only reached ~1/50 of storm level"; Egal et al. (also cited) report a peak ZHR of about 27 against predictions of a possible storm, and record that the main peak required ejection speeds four times the typical cometary value. "Width" is not supported by anything in the two cited papers either. A defender holding Ye & Vaubaillon can show our own source contradicting our own sentence.
findings.fix: Replace the clause with: "The outburst arrived in the early hours of 31 May 2022, within minutes of the 2001 and 2008 timings, though at a fraction of the rate the same models had allowed for — Ye and Vaubaillon put the activity at about a fiftieth of storm level. The timing is the part that was booked in advance and cashed."

findings.field: sources[] label for Spurný et al. (line 419); same implication in refutation §2 (line 209)
findings.problem: The source label reads "Asher & Clube, QJRAS 34:481 (1993), whose predicted encounter years 1995, 1998, 2005 and 2008 were confirmed by Asher & Izumi, MNRAS 297:23 (1998)". A 1998 paper cannot confirm encounters in 2005 and 2008. Spurný et al., which we cite for this chain, says something different and checkable: "Asher & Clube (1993) predicted that future encounters would occur in 1995, 1998, 2005, and 2008" and, separately, "Asher & Izumi (1998) showed that enhanced Taurid activity indeed occurred in the years when the center of the swarm was less than 40° in mean anomaly from the Earth" — a retrospective test against historical records, not a confirmation of the four forward years. Line 209 ("Asher and Izumi showed in 1998 that the enhancements had fallen in the years the model named") carries the same implication by adjacency. This is the same overclaim our own docstring note 5 warns about for 2015, made in a different place.
findings.fix: Sources label: "...inside the 7:2 Jupiter resonance proposed by Asher & Clube, QJRAS 34:481 (1993), who predicted encounters in 1995, 1998, 2005 and 2008; Asher & Izumi, MNRAS 297:23 (1998) showed that historical enhancements had fallen in the years the same swarm criterion picks out." Body line 209: "...predicted enhanced encounters in 1995, 1998, 2005 and 2008; Asher and Izumi tested the criterion backwards in 1998 and found the historical enhancements sitting in the years it names."

findings.field: refutation §1 (line 200) and sources[] label for Wiegert et al. (line 424)
findings.problem: "returned in December 2011 with a zenithal hourly rate near 50, from a radiant displaced from the classical one" — and the source label repeats "from a displaced radiant". Wiegert, Brown, Weryk & Wong (AJ 145:70, 2013), the paper we cite, says the opposite about the word "classical": "The radiant at RA +18° and Dec +56° is typical of the 'classical' Andromedids of the early 1800's." What the 2011 radiant is displaced FROM is the 1872/1885 storm radiant at RA +27°, Dec +44°. Our sentence therefore reports the cited paper as saying the reverse of what it says, in the same breath as the storm dates we take from it. The underlying point — the radiant moved relative to the storms — survives intact, which is why this is a one-clause fix rather than an argument problem.
findings.fix: Body: "...returned in December 2011 with a zenithal hourly rate near 50, from a radiant some 9° in right ascension and 12° in declination away from the 1872/1885 storm radiant — back where the 'classical' Andromedids of the early 1800s were — the whole shift reproduced by integrating dust released at 3D/Biela's 1649 perihelion passage." Source label: "...a December 2011 return at ZHR ≈ 50 from a radiant displaced from the 1872/1885 storm radiant and matching the 'classical' early-1800s one, modelled from dust released at 3D/Biela's 1649 perihelion passage."

findings.problem: "a shower with no calendar history at all". Egal et al., which we cite two lines later, states the contrary: "We find that ordinary cometary activity could have produced other TAH apparitions observed in the past, including in 1930 and 2017." The τ-Herculids are IAU shower #61 with a catalogued annual activity period. The true and stronger claim is about the 1995 material, not about the shower.
findings.fix: "...its date fixed twenty-one years in advance by where two orbits would intersect — and fixed for material that did not exist as a stream before the 1995 break-up, whatever the shower's own thin history of apparitions in 1930 and 2017."

findings.problem: The 22% pole-over-equator figure is transplanted across populations. Robertson et al. (PSJ 2:88, 2021) is titled "Latitude Variation of Flux and Impact Angle of Asteroid Collisions with Earth and the Moon" and models the Granvik near-Earth ASTEROID population: "the flux of impacts to the poles for Earth is 22% greater than the flux at the equator, and 55% greater for the Moon." In the verdict_challenge it is deployed against the geographic reading of "Micrometeor isotropy" — i.e. as a statement about the latitude distribution of small-particle fallout, which the paper does not measure or model. The §3 use (fireball geography) is closer to the modelled population but still not the same one.
findings.fix: In verdict_challenge: "...it is also not exactly true even for larger bodies, where the modelled asteroid impact flux at the poles runs about 22% above the equatorial value (Robertson et al. 2021); no comparable latitude flatness has been demonstrated for the micrometeoroid influx either." In §3, add "for metre-scale and larger impactors" after "the modelled flux".

findings.problem: assessed=True with drifted=True and drift_type="unsourced_addition" feeds a site-wide published figure: build.py counts hedge_drifted, render.py prints it as "N overstated", and the per-entry block renders under the heading "The list overstates its own source" with the labels "The list says" / "The source says" and the subhead "We answer the original above, not the one-line version." But this entry states, correctly and twice, that the Sungenis sentence is NOT this cluster's source — the gloss says it "is not evidence of origination, so the cluster still credits nobody", and clusters.py keeps originator=None. So a reader of the rendered frame is told Sungenis is "its own source" and "the original", and the aggregate count absorbs one case where no descent is claimed. The caveat exists (the bolded "Condition, stated rather than buried" paragraph) but it is inside the note, below the frame that already made the claim.
findings.fix: Keep drifted=True (the finding is real and worth publishing) but move the condition to the front of the note, so the first words under the heading scope it: "Read the heading with one qualification: this is the nearest located text, not a demonstrated source. The specimen carries no citation for these three items — it carries none for any of the 461 — so what follows is a content comparison, not a chain of descent. With that said: the one located ancestor puts meteor showers on the other side's ledger. ..." Alternatively raise the question with the operator of whether the render heading should read "The list overstates the nearest text we could locate" when the cluster's originator is None.

findings.problem: The diurnal-aberration point is asserted rather than argued, and by the page's own logic in the same paragraph it does not obviously survive: if "radiants and speeds are relative quantities" and a moving-sky model relabels the Earth's 29.8 km/s, it relabels the observer's ~0.4 km/s rotational term the same way — the measured relative velocity is unchanged and the correction is equally required in either picture. The preemptive locks this in as one of three things that "may not be softened", so a defender who spots it in one sentence knocks over a load-bearing third of the closing paragraph. (The physics is not wrong — meteor orbit reductions do carry zenith attraction, gravitational acceleration and diurnal aberration terms — but the entry cites nothing for it and never says why relabelling fails here when it succeeds everywhere else in the paragraph.)
findings.fix: Either cut the third survivor to two and let items (i) and (ii) carry the weight, or state the reason the relabelling costs something: "...the last of these being the observer's velocity from the Earth's rotation. A sky that turns instead would have to impose that same 0.4 km/s on every meteoroid already inside the atmosphere, latitude by latitude and hour by hour, and nothing in the moving-sky picture supplies a mechanism that does it." And add a citation for the correction set (Ceplecha's standard reduction) to sources[].

findings.problem: The entry's designated load-bearing claim is technically wrong. It says: "a shell drags its interior uniformly, producing no difference between two satellites at different heights, while the signal Ciufolini and Pavlis extract is precisely the 1/a3 difference between LAGEOS and LAGEOS II", and the advocate block declares this "the only part of the frame-dragging argument that survives the relabelling defence". The Ciufolini-Pavlis observable is not a difference and does not isolate a gradient. Iorio (gr-qc/0412057) Eq. (4) states it verbatim: delta-Omega-dot(LAGEOS) + c1 x delta-Omega-dot(LAGEOS II) = mu_LT x S_LT, with c1 = +0.546 and S_LT = 48.1 mas/yr — a positive-weighted SUM (31 + 0.546 x 31.5 = 48.2), obtained by writing Eq. (5) for both satellites and solving a two-equation system in two unknowns, mu_LT and J2. The combination was "built up in order to cancel out the first even zonal harmonic J2", Iorio's words, not to cancel a constant. A spatially uniform interior dragging Omega_c contributes Omega_c(1 + c1) = 1.546 Omega_c to that observable and is absorbed into mu_LT; with two node rates and one nuisance parameter there is no degree of freedom left to separate a constant from a 1/a3 term.
findings.fix: Replace the functional-form claim with the version that is true and still does the work: (a) general relativity predicts the value of the combination, 48.1 mas/yr, with NO free parameter, from the Earth's independently measured polar moment C and spin rate Omega, whereas a uniform cosmic-drag account has to fit a free constant to the same number; and (b) the 1/a3 scaling is tested by adding a node at a different semimajor axis — LARES, a = 7820 km, predicted Lense-Thirring rate about 118 mas/yr — not by the two LAGEOS satellites alone. Then rewrite the advocate.preemptive paragraph, which currently instructs future editors to protect the incorrect sentence.

findings.problem: Chapter 10 of Vol. I is mischaracterised, and the passages where the source does claim a centre are never met. The entry writes that no metric with a preferred central body "is written down in ch. 10 of Vol. I, which argues instead from the existence of the homogeneous solutions", the tldr says "the rotating solutions this argument leans on fix a direction and not a place", and compression.note says the source's weakness is that "the solutions cited are homogeneous or cylindrically symmetric". In the 2006 scan, ch. 10 "Mathematical Models of a Geocentric Universe" is eleven consecutive shell-dragging sections (Hoyle 594, Einstein 607, Thirring 611, Rosser 616, Bondi 619, Brill and Cohen 623, Moon and Spencer 623, Moller 624, Brown 625, Nightingale 625, Lynden-Bell 626, Barbour and Bertotti 628); the only homogeneous-cosmology material in it is the single Obukhov footnote at p. 608 that the entry itself cites. Worse, the chapter asserts a distinguished centre twice. At p. 623 it quotes Brill and Cohen — "in such a model there cannot be a rotation of the local inertial frame in the center relative to the large masses in the universe" — and concludes "either the shell of 'fixed stars' must be fixed around a rotating center, or the center must be the fixed point for a revolving shell". At ch. 12 p. 711 Bennett adds Barbour and Bertotti: "An object at the center of the hollow sphere will not be affected by the inertial forces. The space around the Earth will exhibit the inertial effects of the distant sphere, but not the Earth itself, if it is centrally located." Cylindrically symmetric solutions the source never cites are answered; the centre claim the source does make is not quoted anywhere in the entry. The Maitra/Wright material also comes from OUR Obukhov 2000 review, not from the source.
findings.fix: Rewrite section 1's framing: say the chapter argues from rotating-SHELL results rather than from rotating cosmologies, quote the Brill and Cohen sentence at p. 623 and the Barbour and Bertotti sentence at p. 711, and answer them — the centre of a shell is distinguished by the shell and not by any body sitting in it; the centrifugal term vanishes along the whole rotation axis, a line, not at a single point; and in the complete-dragging limit "no rotation of the local inertial frame in the center" is the statement that the interior co-rotates, which is the relabelling the entry already concedes two sections later. Keep the homogeneity point for the Obukhov footnote, scoped to it.

findings.field: sources[] (Vol. II entry) / refutation (section 2, light cylinder) / people[]
findings.problem: Misattributed location and author. The sources list says the 2013 Vol. II "ch. 10 carries the Godel material inside the fuller Obukhov quotation", and the refutation says "The book meets this head-on in its 2013 volume" before quoting "sauce for the general relativity goose is sauce for the geocentric gander". In the Vol. II scan, Vol. II ch. 10 is "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism". The Obukhov quotation, the Godel references (Obukhov's "Since the first studies of Lanczos, Gamow and Godel"; Novello/Svaiter/Guimaraes, "Synchronized Frames for Godel's Universe") and the sauce/goose sentence are all on printed p. 647, inside Appendix 1 — "Philosophical and Scientific Ruminations of Martin Selbrede ... As Written in the 1994 Paper 'Geocentricity's Critics Refuse to do Their Homework'". So the superluminal-rotation reply the entry answers is Martin Selbrede's, written in 1994 and reprinted as an appendix, not Sungenis and Bennett's ch. 10 text. Selbrede is separately thanked in Vol. I's front matter for "expertise and consultations". people[] lists only PER-SUNGENIS. On a page whose product is provenance, this is the wrong class of error to carry.
findings.fix: Change the sources line to "Appendix 1, 'Philosophical and Scientific Ruminations of Martin Selbrede', at printed p. 647, carrying the fuller Obukhov quotation, the Godel references and the goose/gander reply". In the refutation, attribute the reply to Selbrede's 1994 paper as reprinted in the 2013 Vol. II rather than to "the book". Note upward that the reply has an author the People tab does not carry. Note also that the 2006 Vol. I answers the superluminal objection in its own voice two pages later, at pp. 615-616, via Rosser — worth citing as the source-side version.

findings.field: clusters.py R05 note and real_source (renders into this entry)
findings.problem: The published page will contradict itself. build.py maps the cluster note to `basis`, and render.py prints `basis` under the verdict chip AND as the summary line of "3 - Refutation". That line currently reads "Frame dragging is real and measured - and is far too small to hold the stars in a daily circuit." The entry's own steelman labels that exact formulation "SURFACE (weak - do not use) ... This loses, and it loses in one move." Alongside it, `real_source_cited` renders "Godel 1949; Lense-Thirring 1918; Gravity Probe B" while the entry's gloss states that Godel is not located in that chapter of the 2006 scan and the docstring notes GP-B's final results postdate the cited work by five years. This is the E01/E03 "recorded, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" pattern the curmudgeon file calls the highest-leverage item on its list; the file's docstring reports it up correctly (note 10), but a report is not a fix and the summary line is on the skim path.
findings.fix: Apply docstring note 10 items (1), (2) and (4) to clusters.py in the same commit as this entry, anchoring the edit on the "R05" cluster key and not on the byte-identical originator= line. Then re-run the two-clocks assertions in tests/test_provenance.py, because build.py dates arguments from real_source and swapping 1949/2011 for 1918/1992/2004 moves the median and the pre-1930 share.

findings.problem: Wrong number. "The claimed balance is out by a factor of about 760, and at the Sun's distance by about 4 x 10^7." The Moon figure is right (757.7). The Sun figure is wrong by three orders of magnitude: on the entry's own constants, omega^2 r at 1 AU = 795.5 m/s2 against GM(Earth)/r2 = 1.781e-8 m/s2, a ratio of 4.47e10. Nothing plausible reproduces 4e7 — using the Sun's own GM instead gives 1.34e5. The docstring's reproduced arithmetic (note 7) contains only the Moon computation, so this figure was added in prose without being computed. It understates our own case, but it is published arithmetic on a page that invites readers to check it.
findings.fix: "and at the Sun's distance by about 4 x 10^10" — or drop the second figure and state the scaling instead, since the mismatch grows as r^3.

findings.problem: The tldr ends on the entry's most contestable move without the qualifier the body insists on. Its closing clause is "setting the Earth's spin to zero makes the prediction exactly zero". The body concedes, correctly and in its own voice, that a well-read geocentrist replies that J is angular momentum relative to the local compass of inertia, that the compass is dragged by the sky in his model, and that "the prediction is unchanged" - "That is correct, and it should be conceded in plain sight." The advocate block rates that same objection as the defender's second-strongest move at survives=4. Readers who never expand the entry carry away the unqualified version, which is the recurring failure the curmudgeon file records for A09, A07, R04, D04 and C08.
findings.fix: End the tldr on what survives the relabelling rather than on the zero. E.g. "...and the defence that rescues it - that the sky drags the compass instead - concedes the Earth turning at one revolution a sidereal day relative to the local inertial compass, measured from orbit to about one part in a hundred."

findings.problem: Unscoped absence claim, in a field the ratchet test does not read. "Nobody in the Lense-Thirring literature makes that claim" is an assertion about an entire corpus made from a sample. tests/test_provenance.py scans tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note and the cluster note; straw_man.detail is not in _blocks, so this passes green - which is exactly the batch-8 finding that the banned construction migrates into unscanned fields. It also sits awkwardly beside our own tldr, which draws an inference of precisely the shape the chapter pre-empts.
findings.fix: Scope it to the texts actually read: "That inference is not made in the papers the chapter itself cites: in Lense and Thirring 1918, in Ciufolini and Pavlis 2004 and in Everitt et al. 2011 the Earth's rotation is an INPUT to the prediction, entering as J = C x Omega, and the measurement tests general relativity given it."

findings.problem: "No physicist since 1905 has held that." — held, that is, that some experiment has proved the Earth to be in absolute motion. Dayton Miller held exactly that: his Mount Wilson interferometry programme ran into the 1930s and his summary paper is titled "The Ether-Drift Experiment and the Determination of the Absolute Motion of the Earth" (Rev. Mod. Phys. 5:203, 1933). He was a credentialed physicist, not a crank on the margins, and he is item 100 of this very list ("Miller aether drift detections."), which our own §6 names. straw_man.detail renders escaped into a published box, so the defender gets to quote our page against our page.
findings.fix: Rescope to the mainstream and name the exception before they do: "...the position attacked is that some experiment has proved the Earth to be in absolute motion. Mainstream physics has not made that claim since 1905, and the last credentialed physicist to press it — Dayton Miller, whose drift claim is item 100 of this same list — is the exception the movement itself cites."

findings.problem: The entry establishes that the DOCTRINE was in the 1992 edition and never tests whether Bouw ORIGINATED it, yet the record credits him and the entry publishes a pedigree ("Where item 310 comes from", "item 310's pedigree runs through a citation Bouw gets right") with no hedge on origination. The entry's own quoted sentence undercuts the credit: at p. 4 Bouw attributes the proposition to "the more subtle physicists", i.e. explicitly to other people — the gloss even says so — and note 6 concedes item 318 cannot be tied to him at all. So one of three items is not his and the other two are, on his own page, someone else's. On a project whose product is provenance and whose README requires origin in three states with "untraced rather than guessed" as a live option, that omission is the error the C02 correction exists to prevent. (A parallel batch-11 treatment of the same cluster reaches the opposite provenance conclusion; the git history records the double-booking as unresolved, so this is the comparison the merge was deferred for.)
findings.fix: Add to the gloss, in the project's own vocabulary: "What is established here is that the doctrine is Bouw's in print, not that it is Bouw's in origin. He attributes the proposition on p. 4 to 'the more subtle physicists', item 318 could not be located in this text at all, and no earlier claimant was tested in this pass — so the origination credit in our record is provisional and is published as such." Report the originator field upward rather than editing it here.

findings.field: clusters.py R11 note (renders as the `basis` line beside the verdict chip)
findings.problem: The summary line readers see before expanding says Bouw "conceded his model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism and must therefore be chosen on theological grounds." That states as Bouw's settled position one horn of the contradiction this entry exists to expose, and the entry's §3 says the opposite — that he asserts a falsifiable cosmology in the body of the book. The source backs §3: p. 3 "every fundamental experiment ever devised to measure the speed of the earth through space measures a speed of zero"; p. 4 "the geocentric evidence is overwhelming"; p. 523 "Geocentricity predicts that earth's lack of motion is absolute"; p. 556 the chapter-36 phenomena "point to a geocentric universe"; p. 539 "the preponderance of geocentric evidence in cosmology has finally forced a geocentric-type model". The theological concession is real but narrow — the Earth-versus-Milky-Way residual at p. 556 and the Bible-believer sufficiency claim at p. 15 — and the note generalises it into Bouw's whole position. This is recurring failure #5, in the highest-traffic field on the entry.
findings.fix: Replace with a note that states both horns: "Bouw states the symmetry himself — dynamical proofs 'are not proofs of anything; nor are they proofs against the geocentric universe' — and elsewhere in the same book calls the geocentric evidence overwhelming and reports his model as making predictions that experiments confirm. The list files the first claim as a proof while spending the second. Where the astronomical evidence runs out, at the Earth-versus-Galaxy gap, he names Scripture as what closes it."

findings.problem: Two printed-page locators are off by one. I settled both from rendered page images, not OCR. (a) The Sagnac sentence — "been performed accurately enough to discern the period of absolute rotation of the firmament is the sidereal day" — is on printed p. 522 (running head "522 Chapter 35"); p. 523 begins with the head "Rotation 523" further down the leaf. The "Geocentricity predicts..." quotes in the same sentence of our text ARE on p. 523, so the refutation attributes two quotes a page apart to one page. (b) The Milky-Way / Scripture concession — "could just as well be viewed as located at the center of the cosmic shells ... But that is where Scripture comes into play" — is on printed p. 556 (running head "556 Chapter 36"), not p. 555; it is the closing paragraph of chapter 36 and the chapter ends on that page.
findings.fix: In §3, split the citation: "...at p. 523 the model is stated as making predictions in so many words ... and, a page earlier, Sagnac interferometry is said to have 'been performed accurately enough...' (p. 522)." Change "(ch. 36, p. 555)" to "(ch. 36, p. 556)" in the steelman and in §5's reference to chapter 36. In sources[0].label, change "Sagnac and the firmament's rotation p. 523" to "the firmament's predicted rotation p. 523 and the Sagnac sidereal-day claim p. 522", and "the Milky-Way concession p. 555" to "p. 556".

findings.problem: The TLDR says the construction's "Earth-near-centre versions were in severe tension with the data by 2011", flat. The body's own limit paragraph says the opposite about scope: "What is established is narrower than 'we are not near a centre': it is that the specific Gpc-scale inhomogeneous models proposed as a replacement for dark energy do badly against the data" — and it quotes Zibin & Moss saying the headline kSZ constraint is "considerably weakened (though still impressive)". The TLDR generalises from dark-energy-replacement void models to all Earth-near-centre versions and drops the caveat the body was careful to publish. This is the recurring TLDR-outruns-body pattern, in the field readers see first and may never expand past.
findings.fix: "...and whose Gpc-scale void versions — the ones proposed as a replacement for dark energy — were in severe tension with the data by 2011."

findings.problem: Bouw's own hedge on the Ellis material is nowhere recorded, and it runs in two directions at once. At p. 539 he writes that "Ellis' model has become an oddity among cosmological models, and it is not without its problems; but it is interesting to see that the preponderance of geocentric evidence in cosmology has finally forced a geocentric-type model, albeit the earth is there placed opposite the center." So (i) he qualifies the very construction we present his citation as cleanly transmitting, and (ii) he reads it not as underdetermination but as evidence forcing a conclusion — which is nearer the opposite of item 310 and is stronger support for our verdict than anything in §6. Separately, the p. 92 quotation that chapter 36 note 2 actually attaches to is Ellis on the cosmological principle being "assumed for a priori reasons and not tested by observation", not the abstract's equivalence result; our gloss reads as though note 2 carries the construction.
findings.fix: In the gloss, after the note-2 sentence: "The note is attached to a different Ellis sentence — the cosmological principle is 'assumed for a priori reasons and not tested by observation' — and where Bouw discusses the construction itself, at pp. 538–539, he calls it 'an oddity among cosmological models' that 'is not without its problems', reading it as a model the evidence 'finally forced' rather than as one of several that fit. That last reading is the tension in a sentence: a claim that the evidence decides, printed twenty pages from the claim that nothing can." Add the hedge to compression.note.

findings.problem: "Appendix E derives the rotating-frame accelerations (eq. 11) and stops there" is false about the appendix's contents, and preemptive (a) insists this claim "must stay a statement about what the appendix contains". It does not stop: immediately after the p. 746 sentence we quote, Bouw writes "Of course, equation (11) is kinematic, not dynamic and we have to show the geocentric model is dynamically correct. To do that, all we have to do is to multiply both sides by the star's mass, m", producing eq. (12) F = ma, and then applies it to the sun, moon, planets, artificial satellites, stars and to light propagation. Worse for §3: the appendix OPENS (pp. 740–741, eqs. 1–3) by arguing that the kinematic/dynamic distinction is a "sleight of hand" — multiplying one side by m/m — which is Bouw's pre-emptive answer to our "his cosmos is not a relabelling", and it goes unengaged. Not published (build strips advocate to review/advocate.json), but it is the stated reason we run no fit against Bouw's model, so it will misdirect the next editor.
findings.fix: Correct the note to what is true: "Appendix E (pp. 740–747) ends at F = ma for a single star (eq. 12); no field equation, stress-energy tensor or cosmological solution appears anywhere in it, so there is no fit to run." And add one sentence to §3 answering the m/m argument on its merits: what makes the model dynamical is not the factor of m but the claim at p. 5 that a superdense medium "physically controls all motion" and at p. 746 that its gravitational field is what holds the star in place — a medium with a gravitational field is not a bookkeeping convention, whichever side of the equation the mass sits on.

findings.problem: The p. 4 quotation is elided as "The more subtle physicists … will claim, with some justification...". What the ellipsis removes is not connective tissue but the clause "many of whom know well that the geocentric evidence is overwhelming" — from inside the quoted sentence, and it substantially weakens the hedged reading we build on it. The gloss does disclose the clause, but locates it as "the same page", which understates the cut: it is the same sentence, indeed the elided span. compression.source_wording repeats the elision with no disclosure at all, and that block is the side-by-side comparison a reader uses to check us. Given that this entry's own standing rule is not to commit the compression sin in our favour, the elision needs to be visible where the comparison is made.
findings.fix: In the gloss change "the same page tells the reader" to "the elided clause itself tells the reader", and quote it in place: "The more subtle physicists, [many of whom know well that the geocentric evidence is overwhelming,] will claim, with some justification...". Restore the bracketed clause to compression.source_wording so the comparison block shows what was cut.

findings.problem: Two absence claims are asserted unscoped, in fields the ratchet test reads. "No result in this literature locates a planet" is a claim about an entire literature made from five papers; "That result was never retracted" is a claim about the whole record of a journal. Both are substantively right, and neither matches the banned regex — which is precisely the failure the last sweep described as "writers have learned the regex, not the rule". The house rule is to name the text searched.
findings.fix: "None of the results cited above — Alnes & Amarzguioui, Caldwell & Stebbins, Clarkson/Bassett/Lu, Zhang & Stebbins, Moss/Zibin/Scott — constrains an observer's position at better than megaparsec resolution; at that resolution the Earth and the Milky Way are the same point." And: "No retraction or erratum is attached to the paper on the publisher's record page, which is where we looked."
